When a [small business](/articles/tag/small-business) starts operating, much of its knowledge may exist in the owner's head, email messages, spreadsheets or informal conversations. That arrangement can feel manageable when the business is small, but it becomes harder to maintain as customers, suppliers, employees and responsibilities increase.

Business documentation provides a more reliable way to record important information, explain how work should be done and preserve decisions for future reference.

For South African small businesses, documentation is not simply an administrative exercise. Certain records are required by law, while other documents help the business operate consistently, communicate clearly and reduce avoidable misunderstandings.

The right documents depend on the business's structure, industry, workforce and activities. This guide explains the practical benefits of professional documentation, which records to consider and how to create a manageable system.

## 1. It clarifies responsibilities and expectations

Unclear responsibilities can cause delays, duplicated work and disagreements. A written document helps people understand what is expected, who is responsible and what should happen next.

For example, a small company might document:

- Who approves purchases and payments.
- How customer enquiries are handled.
- What information must be collected before work begins.
- How complaints are escalated.
- Who checks work before delivery.
- How staff request leave or report an absence.

The appropriate format depends on the purpose. A short procedure may be sufficient for a routine task, while a formal employment document or agreement may need more careful drafting and professional review.

The objective is to make expectations clear enough that people do not have to rely entirely on memory or repeated verbal instructions.

## 2. It supports consistent service delivery

Customers generally expect a business to provide a reasonably consistent experience, even when different people handle their enquiries or fulfil their orders.

Documented procedures can help a business repeat important tasks reliably. A quotation process, for example, might specify the information required from a customer, how costs are checked, who approves the quotation and how the final version is sent.

Useful operational documents can include:

- Customer enquiry procedures.
- Quotation and approval workflows.
- Service delivery checklists.
- Quality-control checklists.
- Complaint-handling procedures.
- Handover notes.
- Supplier onboarding procedures.

Not every task needs a lengthy policy. A clear one-page checklist may be more effective than a complicated manual that nobody uses.

Review procedures when the business changes its systems, services or responsibilities. Documentation should reflect how the business is actually meant to operate, rather than becoming an outdated collection of files.

## 3. It preserves important business information

Small companies often depend heavily on a few individuals. If important information exists only in one person's inbox, personal device or memory, it may be difficult to retrieve when that person is unavailable.

An organised record-keeping system helps preserve important information and makes it easier for authorised people to locate what they need.

Depending on the business, records may include:

- Customer and supplier agreements.
- Quotations, invoices and payment records.
- Business correspondence.
- Meeting minutes and decisions.
- Project specifications and approvals.
- Employee records.
- Tax and accounting documents.
- [Policies and procedures](/articles/tag/policies-and-procedures).

The system can be digital, paper-based or a combination of both. What matters is that records are accurate, appropriately protected, organised and retrievable.

South African businesses should pay particular attention to their legal record-keeping duties. The [South African Revenue Service's record-keeping guidance](https://www.sars.gov.za/client-segments/record-keeping/) explains who must keep records, how they should be maintained and the relevant retention requirements for tax purposes.

> **Organise your business documents:** Visit [Mogen Services](/services) to explore its business and digital services and consider what documentation support may suit your needs.

## 4. It helps businesses understand their obligations

Professional documentation can support compliance, but having a document does not automatically make a business compliant. The document must be appropriate, accurate, implemented and kept current.

Different obligations apply to different businesses. For example, tax record requirements are not identical to company record requirements, employment obligations or rules governing personal information.

### Tax and accounting records

[SARS](/articles/tag/sars) provides guidance on records that taxpayers must maintain. The applicable retention period depends on the circumstances and the type of record. For many records connected with a submitted tax return, the general period is five years, but exceptions and longer retention requirements can apply, including where an audit or investigation is ongoing.

Businesses should consult the relevant [SARS record-keeping requirements](https://www.sars.gov.za/client-segments/record-keeping/) rather than assuming that every document can be discarded after a fixed period.

### Company records

Companies must maintain certain records under the Companies Act. The Companies and Intellectual Property Commission (CIPC) explains that required records include the company's Memorandum of Incorporation and applicable amendments, as well as specified company, director, shareholder-meeting and financial records.

CIPC identifies a seven-year retention period for several categories of company records. This is not a universal retention period for every business document.

Review the official [CIPC company records guidance](https://www.cipc.co.za/?page_id=15683) to understand the categories relevant to your company.

### Personal information

Businesses that collect or use personal information should also consider their obligations under the Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA).

Relevant documentation may include privacy notices, internal procedures for handling personal information, access controls, retention practices and records of how information is processed. The appropriate measures depend on the organisation and the information involved.

Consult the [Information Regulator of South Africa](https://inforegulator.org.za/) for official guidance.

Because requirements vary, obtain advice from an appropriately qualified professional when a document affects legal rights, tax obligations, employment or regulatory compliance.

## 5. It improves accountability and decision-making

Written decisions help explain why a business took a particular action and what was agreed.

Meeting minutes, approval records, project sign-offs and documented changes can be especially useful when several people contribute to a decision.

A practical decision record might capture:

- The issue being considered.
- The decision made.
- The person or people responsible for approving it.
- Any actions required.
- The deadline or review date.
- The supporting documents.

This does not mean every informal conversation needs formal minutes. Documentation should be proportionate to the importance and consequences of the decision.

For a significant purchase, a customer contract or a change to a project scope, a written record may prevent later uncertainty about what was agreed.

## 6. It reduces reliance on the business owner

Many small businesses rely on the owner to explain every process, approve every action and remember every commitment. This can become a bottleneck as the business grows.

Documented procedures and responsibilities help the owner delegate routine tasks without losing visibility over important work.

Start by identifying tasks that are repeated frequently. Write down the steps, the information required, the expected result and any decisions that must be escalated.

Then test the instructions with someone who did not create them. If that person cannot follow the process, the documentation may need clearer language, additional examples or a simpler sequence.

This approach can support onboarding, handovers and continuity when staff members are absent or responsibilities change.

## 7. It helps manage disputes and misunderstandings

Disagreements often arise when people have different expectations about scope, payment, responsibilities or deadlines.

Written agreements and approvals can reduce ambiguity by recording what the parties accepted.

For customer work, consider whether the relevant documents clearly explain:

- The work or service being supplied.
- The agreed price and payment terms.
- What the customer must provide.
- Delivery dates or estimated timeframes.
- The process for approving changes.
- Relevant limitations, exclusions and cancellation terms.
- How concerns or disputes will be handled.

The exact requirements depend on the type of transaction and applicable law. A generic template may not adequately address a particular arrangement, especially where substantial financial or legal consequences are involved.

For employment agreements, partnership arrangements and other legally significant documents, professional review may be appropriate. Documentation supports clearer expectations, but it does not guarantee that a dispute will be avoided or that a document will be legally enforceable.

## 8. It creates a foundation for business growth

As a company grows, it may add employees, suppliers, services, locations or larger customers. The informal processes that worked at the beginning may no longer be sufficient.

A basic documentation framework can make expansion easier by establishing repeatable ways of working.

For example, a growing service company might develop:

- A consistent customer onboarding process.
- Standard quotation and approval procedures.
- Project handover checklists.
- Supplier assessment records.
- Staff onboarding materials.
- Version-controlled policies.
- A central location for approved templates.

The aim is not to produce paperwork for its own sake. It is to reduce confusion as more people become involved in the business.

A small company should build the level of documentation it can realistically maintain. A few clear, current documents are often more useful than a large manual full of duplicated or obsolete information.

## 9. It makes information easier to protect and retrieve

Professional documentation also involves deciding where information is stored, who can access it and how changes are controlled.

A folder full of documents is not necessarily an effective record system. Files with unclear names, duplicate versions and unrestricted access can create new risks.

A simple structure can include:

- Clear folder names by business function.
- Consistent file naming.
- Version numbers or revision dates for controlled documents.
- Restricted access to confidential records.
- Backups and a documented recovery process.
- A record of who approves important changes.
- A retention and disposal process based on applicable requirements.

For electronic records, consider access controls, security and whether the information can be retrieved when needed. Sensitive information should not be shared broadly merely because it is convenient.

Keep only the personal information necessary for legitimate purposes, apply appropriate safeguards and follow relevant legal requirements. Do not adopt a blanket retention period for all records without checking the rules that apply to each category.

## 10. It makes onboarding and handovers more manageable

When a new employee, contractor or business partner joins, they need to understand how the organisation works.

A structured onboarding pack can provide relevant information without requiring the owner or manager to repeat every explanation.

Depending on the role, it might include:

- An introduction to the business and its services.
- Responsibilities and reporting arrangements.
- Relevant workplace policies.
- Standard operating procedures.
- Required forms and approval routes.
- Information security and confidentiality expectations.
- Contact details for support.

Only provide documents appropriate to the recipient's role, and take care with confidential information.

The same principle applies when handing work from one person to another. A project handover document should explain the current status, decisions already made, outstanding tasks, important contacts and the location of relevant files.

## How to start building a practical documentation system

You do not need to write every policy and procedure at once. Start with the records that are legally required or most important to daily operations.

### Step 1: Inventory the documents you already have

Gather existing agreements, forms, procedures, financial records and policies. Identify duplicates, outdated versions and documents that are difficult to locate.

Do not delete records simply because they look old. Check applicable retention requirements before disposing of them.

### Step 2: Separate legal requirements from operational preferences

Create two lists:

- Documents or records that the business is required to maintain.
- Documents that would make its operations clearer or more consistent.

Consult official guidance and qualified advisers where necessary. This prevents a useful internal checklist from being mistaken for a legally required document.

### Step 3: Prioritise high-impact gaps

Start with missing documents that could cause serious confusion or operational difficulty. These might include customer agreements, payment approval procedures, essential records or instructions for handling personal information.

The priority will depend on your business model and risks.

### Step 4: Assign ownership

Decide who is responsible for creating, approving, updating and storing each document. Include a review date where appropriate.

A policy without an owner can quickly become outdated. A clear responsibility makes maintenance more likely.

> **Review your business needs:** Visit [Mogen Business Documentation](/services/business-documentation) to explore available services and consider whether your business documentation needs a more structured approach.

### Step 5: Use consistent templates

Templates can help maintain consistent headings, document identifiers, dates and approval details. However, a template should be reviewed for relevance and accuracy before use.

Do not assume that a document downloaded from the internet is appropriate for every [South African business](/articles/tag/south-african-business) or industry.

### Step 6: Review and improve

Ask the people who use the documents whether they can understand and follow them. Remove unnecessary complexity, clarify ambiguous instructions and update the documents when processes change.

## Conclusion

Professional business documentation helps small companies preserve important information, communicate expectations, maintain consistent processes and prepare for growth. It can also support legal and regulatory responsibilities when the documents and record-keeping practices are appropriate to the business.

The most effective approach is practical rather than bureaucratic: understand what you must keep, document important recurring processes, protect confidential information and ensure that records remain accurate and accessible to authorised people.

Start with the documents that matter most to your operations, then build a manageable system that can grow with the business.

Many small businesses keep documents for one of two reasons: they might need them again, or they are worried that deleting them could cause a problem.

The result is often an inconsistent filing system. Invoices are stored in several folders, old customer information remains in email accounts, contracts are difficult to locate and nobody knows which documents can safely be deleted.

Keeping every document forever is not a practical solution.

It increases storage requirements, makes information harder to find and can create unnecessary privacy and security risks. On the other hand, deleting important records too early can make it difficult to respond to tax queries, audits, disputes or company administration requirements.

South African businesses need a structured approach to deciding what to keep, why it must be retained, where it should be stored and when it can be disposed of.

A [record retention](/articles/tag/record-retention) schedule provides that structure.

It is particularly important to understand that there is no single retention period that applies to every business document. Different laws and business circumstances can impose different requirements.

Three important starting points are the South African Revenue Service's record-keeping requirements, section 24 of the Companies Act and section 14 of the Protection of Personal Information Act ([POPIA](/articles/tag/popia)).

## What is a record retention schedule?

A record retention schedule is a document that explains how long different categories of business records should be kept and what should happen when the applicable retention period ends.

It normally identifies:

- The type of record.
- Why the business keeps it.
- Which legal or operational requirement applies.
- How long it must be retained.
- When the retention period begins.
- Who is responsible for the record.
- Where it is stored.
- Who may access it.
- How it should be securely disposed of.

The schedule turns [record keeping](/articles/tag/record-keeping) from an informal habit into a managed business process.

It also helps employees understand that a document should not be deleted simply because it is old or difficult to organise.

## 1. Understand the SARS record-keeping period

The [SARS](/articles/tag/sars) record-keeping rules are an important starting point for businesses that submit tax returns.

SARS explains that taxpayers must keep records, books of account and supporting documents so that they can demonstrate compliance with tax requirements.

Its published guidance generally requires a person who has submitted a return to retain the relevant records for five years, counting from the date the return was submitted.

The exact treatment depends on the taxpayer's circumstances.

For example:

- A person who submitted a return generally retains the relevant records for five years from submission.
- A person required to submit a return but who has not done so may need to retain records indefinitely after the initial five-year period until the return is submitted.
- A person who was not required to submit a return but received income or engaged in taxable activity has separate retention considerations.
- Records connected to an audit or investigation must be retained until that process is concluded.
- Records connected to an objection or appeal may need to be retained until the disputed matter becomes final.

These distinctions are important. A business should not simply calculate five years from the date an invoice was issued and assume that the document can then be deleted.

The relevant trigger may be the date a return was submitted, the end of a tax period or the conclusion of an audit or dispute.

SARS also states that records must be kept in their original form, in an orderly fashion, in a safe place and available for inspection, audit or investigation.

Electronic records may be kept in the form prescribed by the Commissioner. SARS identifies circumstances in which taxpayers must request authorisation to keep records in a different form or at a physical location outside [South Africa](/articles/tag/south-africa).

The current [SARS record-keeping guidance](https://www.sars.gov.za/client-segments/record-keeping/) was updated on 19 August 2026.

## 2. Understand the Companies Act seven-year requirement

Businesses operating through companies also need to consider section 24 of the Companies Act 71 of 2008.

Section 24(1) states that documents, accounts, books, writings, records or other information that a company is required to keep under the Act or another public regulation must be kept:

- In written form, or in another form that can be converted into written form within a reasonable time.
- For seven years, or for any longer period specified in another applicable public regulation.

Section 24 also identifies specific company records that must be maintained.

These include:

- The company's Memorandum of Incorporation and amendments.
- Records of current and past directors.
- Reports presented at annual general meetings.
- Annual financial statements.
- Accounting records.
- Notices and minutes of shareholders' meetings.
- Shareholder resolutions and related documents.
- Certain written communications to holders of securities.
- Minutes and resolutions of directors and relevant committees.

The Act also specifies that accounting records must be maintained for the current financial year and the previous seven completed financial years.

This is an important distinction.

The seven-year period is not simply a replacement for every other retention rule. It applies to company records required under the Act or another public regulation, and specific records have their own wording and retention requirements.

A sole proprietor is not automatically subject to every company-record requirement in section 24 simply because the business operates in South Africa. The business's legal structure matters.

You can consult the official [Companies Act 71 of 2008](https://www.justice.gov.za/legislation/acts/2008-071.pdf), particularly section 24.

## 3. Understand POPIA's retention limitation

Record retention is not only about keeping information long enough.

Businesses must also consider when personal information should no longer be retained.

Section 14 of POPIA deals with the retention and restriction of records containing personal information.

It states that personal information should not be retained for longer than is necessary to achieve the purpose for which it was collected or subsequently processed, subject to specified exceptions.

These exceptions include circumstances where:

- Retention is required or authorised by law.
- The responsible party reasonably requires the record for lawful purposes related to its functions or activities.
- Retention is required by a contract.
- The data subject has consented to the retention.

Section 14 also addresses what happens when the business is no longer authorised to retain the information. The responsible party must destroy or delete the record, or de-identify it, as soon as reasonably practicable. Destruction or deletion must prevent reconstruction in an intelligible form.

This creates an important balance.

A business should not delete tax records merely because they contain personal information and a general retention period has passed if another law still requires the records to be retained.

Equally, it should not keep every customer enquiry, identification document or marketing contact indefinitely just because the business might find the information useful one day.

The business needs to understand both the legal retention obligation and the purpose for which personal information is being held.

Read [POPIA section 14 in the official Act](https://www.justice.gov.za/legislation/acts/2013-004.pdf).

## 4. Why five years and seven years are not contradictory

A common record-keeping question is whether a [South African business](/articles/tag/south-african-business) should retain documents for five years or seven years.

The answer depends on which requirement applies to the particular record.

SARS's guidance describes tax-related retention periods. The Companies Act imposes requirements on records that companies must keep under that Act or other public regulation.

A company may therefore have records that fall under both sets of requirements.

Where more than one legal requirement applies, the business must comply with all of them. In practice, this may mean retaining a particular record for the longer applicable period.

However, it would be inaccurate to say that every document belonging to every business must automatically be kept for seven years.

The business should identify the applicable law, record category and retention trigger before deciding when to dispose of it.

The following table is a planning aid, not a complete legal retention schedule:

| Record category | Important starting point |
| --- | --- |
| Tax returns and supporting documents | Generally five years from return submission under SARS guidance, subject to exceptions |
| Company records required by the Companies Act | Generally seven years under section 24, or longer where another rule applies |
| Company accounting records | Current financial year plus previous seven completed financial years |
| Customer personal information | No longer than necessary for the relevant purpose, subject to section 14 exceptions and other laws |
| Records under audit or investigation | Retain until the relevant process is concluded where required |

Do not use this table as a reason to delete records without checking the underlying legal requirements.

## 5. Create categories for your business records

A retention schedule becomes easier to manage when records are grouped into understandable categories.

A small business might use the following structure:

**Financial and tax records**

- Sales invoices.
- Purchase invoices.
- Receipts.
- Bank statements.
- Payment confirmations.
- Tax returns.
- Tax assessments.
- SARS correspondence.
- VAT and payroll-related records where applicable.

**Company and governance records**

- Incorporation documents.
- Memorandum of Incorporation.
- Director records.
- Shareholder records.
- Meeting minutes.
- Resolutions.
- Annual financial statements.

**Customer and supplier records**

- Contracts.
- Service agreements.
- Purchase orders.
- Supplier information.
- Customer correspondence.
- Complaints and dispute records.

**Employment records**

- Employment agreements.
- Payroll information.
- Leave records.
- Disciplinary documentation.
- Training records.
- Relevant correspondence.

**Operational records**

- Policies and procedures.
- Standard operating procedures.
- Project records.
- Quality-control records.
- Asset registers.
- Insurance documentation.

**Marketing and communication records**

- Newsletter subscriber information.
- Marketing consent records.
- Campaign records.
- Customer communication preferences.
- Unsubscribe and objection records.

These categories are not all governed by the same retention period. The schedule should identify the requirements applicable to each one.

## 6. Build the retention schedule

Once the business has identified its record categories, create a schedule that can be used consistently.

A useful template includes the following fields:

| Field | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| Record category | The type of document or information |
| Purpose | Why the business needs the record |
| Legal or operational basis | The law, contract or legitimate business requirement |
| Retention period | How long the record must be kept |
| Trigger date | The event that starts the retention period |
| Responsible person | Who manages the record |
| Storage location | Where the record is held |
| Access level | Who may view or change it |
| Disposal method | How it will be securely destroyed or deleted |
| Review date | When the schedule should be checked again |

A schedule should be understandable to the people who use it.

Avoid vague instructions such as "keep important documents permanently" or "delete old records after five years".

Instead, identify the document category and the applicable trigger.

For example, a tax record may need to be retained for a period calculated from the submission of a return rather than from the date on the document itself.

## 7. Organise electronic records properly

Electronic storage can make record management easier, but only when the information is organised and retrievable.

A folder containing thousands of files with names such as `scan001.pdf`, `invoice-final-new.pdf` and `document-copy.pdf` is not an effective records management system.

Use a consistent naming convention.

For example:

    ```text
    2026-10-31_supplier-name_invoice_001.pdf
    2026-10-31_customer-name_service-agreement.pdf
    2026-10-31_company_directors-resolution.pdf
    ```

The date should follow a consistent format, and the filename should identify the document without exposing unnecessary personal information.

Organise folders by category, financial year, project or another structure that reflects how the business retrieves information.

Consider:

- Restricting access to sensitive records.
- Maintaining secure backups.
- Keeping important documents in their original form.
- Using version control for policies and agreements.
- Avoiding uncontrolled copies across personal devices.
- Ensuring that records can be exported or reproduced when needed.
- Recording changes to important company documents.

SARS's requirements for orderly and safe record keeping are relevant when designing an electronic filing system.

Businesses should also understand where their electronic records are physically stored. SARS identifies records kept outside South Africa as a circumstance that may require authorisation under its record-retention process.

If a cloud provider is involved, establish where the records are stored and obtain appropriate tax or legal guidance on the applicable requirements.

## 8. Assign responsibility for each category

A retention schedule will not work if nobody is responsible for maintaining it.

A small business may not have a dedicated records manager. That does not prevent it from assigning responsibility.

For example:

- The owner or director may oversee company records.
- The bookkeeper may manage financial and tax documentation.
- An HR administrator may manage employment records.
- A designated employee may manage customer correspondence.
- A system administrator may manage storage permissions and backups.

These roles should be assigned according to the actual structure of the business.

Where an external accountant, payroll provider or document storage provider maintains records, the business should understand what is held, where it is held and how it can be retrieved.

Outsourcing record storage does not remove the need for the business to understand its obligations.

## 9. Create a secure disposal process

A retention schedule should explain what happens when a record reaches the end of its applicable retention period.

It should not rely on employees independently deciding which files look old enough to delete.

A controlled disposal process could include:

1. Identify records approaching their review date.
2. Check whether an audit, investigation, objection, appeal or dispute is still active.
3. Confirm that no other legal or contractual retention requirement applies.
4. Check whether personal information remains necessary for a lawful purpose.
5. Obtain approval from the person responsible for the record category.
6. Delete or destroy the records securely where authorised.
7. Record what was disposed of and when.

For physical records, secure shredding or an appropriate destruction service may be necessary.

For electronic records, deletion should consider active storage, synchronised copies and backups. The business should understand whether deleted records remain recoverable and how backup retention is managed.

POPIA section 14 requires destruction or deletion to be carried out in a manner that prevents reconstruction in an intelligible form.

Do not delete records that are subject to a legal hold, audit or active dispute simply because the normal retention date has arrived.

## 10. Review the schedule when the business changes

A retention schedule should be reviewed periodically.

It may need updating when:

- The business changes its legal structure.
- A new service or product is introduced.
- The business begins employing staff.
- The business registers for additional tax obligations.
- A new contract imposes record-keeping requirements.
- The business starts collecting additional personal information.
- A new system or cloud provider is introduced.
- A relevant law or regulation changes.

A small business that begins as a sole proprietorship may later become a company. Its record-keeping requirements may change as a result.

Similarly, a business that introduces customer accounts or online subscriptions may begin processing more personal information and need clearer retention and deletion procedures.

Review the schedule at least annually and whenever a significant operational or legal change occurs.

## 11. A practical example for a small business

Imagine a growing service business that operates from a small office and serves customers in areas such as [Maboloka](/locations/maboloka), [Soshanguve](/locations/soshanguve) and [Centurion](/locations/centurion).

It receives enquiries through its website, sends quotations by email, issues invoices, buys materials from suppliers and keeps customer correspondence.

Without a retention schedule, documents may be scattered across:

- A bookkeeping application.
- Email inboxes.
- Shared cloud folders.
- Staff laptops.
- Mobile phones.
- Physical filing cabinets.

The business may also retain customer information long after the original purpose has ended.

A simple records management project would begin by identifying these locations and assigning each record category an owner.

The business could then map tax and company records to the applicable legal requirements, review personal information under POPIA and create a secure disposal process.

The result is not simply a cleaner filing system. It is a more reliable way to retrieve information, demonstrate compliance and reduce unnecessary exposure of personal information.

## 12. Record retention checklist

Use this checklist as a starting point for reviewing your current system:

- [ ] Identify the business's legal structure.
- [ ] List the categories of records the business creates and receives.
- [ ] Identify which records are required for tax purposes.
- [ ] Review Companies Act requirements where the business is a company.
- [ ] Identify personal information held by the business.
- [ ] Establish the purpose and applicable retention basis for personal information.
- [ ] Record the retention period and trigger date for each category.
- [ ] Assign a responsible person to each category.
- [ ] Document where electronic and physical records are stored.
- [ ] Review access permissions and backup arrangements.
- [ ] Create a secure disposal process.
- [ ] Check for audits, investigations, objections, appeals and disputes before disposal.
- [ ] Review the schedule annually and after significant changes.

## Frequently asked questions

### Must every South African business keep records for seven years?

No. Section 24 of the Companies Act applies to company records required under that Act or another public regulation. SARS has separate tax record-keeping requirements, generally involving five-year periods with important exceptions. The applicable period depends on the business and the record.

### Does SARS allow electronic record keeping?

SARS permits electronic records in the form prescribed by the Commissioner. Its guidance also identifies circumstances where authorisation is required, including certain arrangements involving records physically stored outside South Africa.

### Does POPIA mean I must delete customer records after five or seven years?

No. POPIA section 14 is based on the purpose and lawful basis for retaining personal information, subject to exceptions including retention required or authorised by law. It does not establish one universal five- or seven-year period for all personal information.

### Can I delete records while an audit is underway?

You should not dispose of records that must be retained for an active audit or investigation. SARS states that records subject to an audit or investigation must be kept until that process is concluded.

### Should a small business have a written retention policy?

A written policy and schedule make it easier to apply consistent decisions, assign responsibility and demonstrate how records are managed. The level of detail should be appropriate to the business's size, activities and obligations.

## Conclusion

Good record keeping is not about storing every document forever. It is about knowing which records the business needs, why they must be retained and when they can be disposed of.

South African businesses should distinguish between SARS tax requirements, the Companies Act requirements that apply to companies and POPIA's rules for retaining personal information.

A practical record retention schedule brings these requirements into one manageable system. It gives employees clear instructions, helps the business retrieve important information and reduces the risk of retaining personal information without a valid reason.

Start by identifying the records you already hold. Then establish the applicable requirements, assign responsibility and document a secure disposal process.

A consistent system is easier to maintain than a filing cabinet or cloud folder that nobody knows how to manage.

A business website should not only look professional. People should also be able to read its content, navigate its pages and complete important actions regardless of the device or method they use to access it.

Consider a potential customer trying to enquire about a service using a phone with a small screen. Another visitor may use a keyboard instead of a mouse, increase their text size or rely on a screen reader to understand the page. If the website's navigation, buttons or forms are difficult to use, those visitors may struggle to become customers.

[Website accessibility](/articles/tag/website-accessibility) is often treated as a specialist concern reserved for large organisations. In practice, it is relevant to businesses of every size. A small company serving customers around [Maboloka](/locations/maboloka), [Soshanguve](/locations/soshanguve), [Centurion](/locations/centurion) or elsewhere can benefit from making its website clearer, easier to navigate and more predictable.

The World Wide Web Consortium's Web Content [Accessibility](/articles/tag/accessibility) Guidelines ([WCAG](/articles/tag/wcag)) provide an established framework for making web content more accessible. WCAG 2.2 is the current recommendation discussed in this article. Its criteria address a wide range of needs, including visual, auditory, physical and cognitive accessibility.

Accessibility is not a decorative feature that can simply be added at the end of a project. It affects the way a website is planned, designed, developed and maintained.

## What does website accessibility mean?

Website accessibility means designing and developing [websites](/articles/tag/websites) so that people with different abilities can perceive, understand, navigate and interact with the content.

It includes more than adding alternative text to images or choosing readable colours.

An accessible website should consider:

- People who navigate with a keyboard rather than a mouse.
- People who use screen readers or other assistive technologies.
- People with low vision who need sufficient contrast or larger text.
- People who have difficulty distinguishing certain colours.
- People with limited dexterity who may struggle with small controls.
- People who need clear instructions when completing forms.
- People who benefit from captions, transcripts or alternative media.

Accessibility improvements often help visitors who do not identify as having a disability. Clear headings, readable text, predictable navigation and understandable error messages make websites easier for many people to use.

WCAG 2.2 groups its requirements around four principles: content should be perceivable, operable, understandable and robust. These principles provide a useful starting point when reviewing a website.

Read the [W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/) for the complete standard.

## 1. Make navigation work without a mouse

A website should not require visitors to use a mouse for every interaction.

Some people navigate using a keyboard, switch device or another input method. Others may simply prefer keyboard navigation.

A basic keyboard test is straightforward:

1. Open a page.
2. Press the Tab key.
3. Observe which interactive element receives focus.
4. Continue through the links, buttons and form controls.
5. Use Shift + Tab to move backwards.
6. Use Enter or Space where appropriate to activate controls.

The visitor should be able to identify which element is currently selected. This is known as the keyboard focus indicator.

A common design mistake is removing the browser's default focus outline without providing a sufficiently visible alternative. The result may look cleaner to a designer using a mouse, but a keyboard user can lose track of where they are on the page.

Use a visible focus style that contrasts with surrounding content. Also check that sticky navigation bars, cookie notices or floating elements do not completely hide the element receiving focus.

WCAG 2.2 includes a Level AA criterion requiring a focused component not to be entirely hidden by author-created content.

## 2. Use headings to create a logical structure

Headings help visitors understand how a page is organised.

They also help assistive technologies communicate the structure of a page and allow some users to move between sections without reading every paragraph.

A sensible heading hierarchy might look like this:

- H1: The main subject of the page.
- H2: The major sections.
- H3: Supporting topics within a section.

Do not choose heading levels simply because a particular font size looks attractive. Heading levels should describe the document structure, while CSS controls the visual presentation.

For example, a service page might use:

- H1: Website Development
- H2: What the Service Includes
- H2: How the Process Works
- H3: Planning and Requirements
- H3: Design and Development
- H2: Frequently Asked Questions

A page with several visually large headings but no meaningful hierarchy can be difficult to understand, particularly when navigating with assistive technology.

WCAG includes requirements for meaningful page titles, logical focus order, descriptive link purpose and headings that identify their content.

## 3. Make text readable

Text should be easy to distinguish from its background.

A pale grey paragraph on a white background may look subtle in a design mock-up, but it can become difficult to read on a mobile phone in bright sunlight or for someone with reduced contrast sensitivity.

Review:

- Body text colour.
- Heading contrast.
- Navigation labels.
- Button text.
- Form labels and instructions.
- Placeholder text.
- Disabled and error states.

WCAG 2.2 specifies contrast requirements for normal text and large text. As a general Level AA target, normal text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, while large text needs at least 3:1, subject to the standard's exceptions.

Do not communicate important information through colour alone. A red border around an invalid form field, for example, should be accompanied by a clear error message.

Text should also remain usable when visitors increase its size. Avoid fixed-height containers that cut off content or layouts that require unnecessary horizontal scrolling when text is enlarged.

## 4. Give meaningful images appropriate alternatives

Images can communicate important information, demonstrate products and help visitors understand services.

However, not everyone experiences images visually.

Alternative text, commonly called alt text, provides a text equivalent for informative images. It should describe the image's purpose in the context of the page rather than simply list everything visible in the photograph.

Consider a business website showing a completed installation.

A useful alternative might describe the actual installation and the relevant context. A generic description such as "image 1" provides little assistance.

Different images need different treatment:

| Image type | Recommended approach |
| --- | --- |
| Informative photograph | Describe the relevant information or purpose |
| Product image | Identify the product and useful distinguishing detail |
| Linked image | Describe the destination or action |
| Decorative image | Allow assistive technology to ignore it |
| Complex diagram | Provide an appropriate text explanation |

Do not use alt text as an opportunity to repeat keywords. Its primary purpose is to make meaningful image information available to people who cannot see it.

Videos also need consideration. Prerecorded video with audio should generally have appropriate captions, and important visual information may require additional alternatives.

## 5. Design forms that explain what visitors must do

[Contact forms](/articles/tag/contact-forms), quotation requests, booking forms and newsletter registrations are important parts of many business websites.

A form that looks simple can still create accessibility problems.

One common mistake is relying on placeholder text instead of proper labels.

For example, a field that displays "Enter your email address" only inside the input box may lose that instruction once the visitor starts typing. It may also fail to provide the accessible name expected by assistive technology.

Use a properly associated label for each form control.

The W3C's [form labelling tutorial](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/labels/) explains how labels should be connected to their controls.

Good form design should also include:

- Clear identification of required fields.
- Instructions for unusual formats.
- Appropriate input types for email addresses, telephone numbers and dates.
- Helpful validation messages.
- Clear confirmation when a submission succeeds.
- An explanation of what happens after submission.

Avoid asking for information that is not necessary to process the enquiry.

### Make error messages useful

A message such as "Invalid input" does not explain what the visitor should correct.

A better message identifies the problem and gives an understandable next step.

For example:

- "Enter a valid email address."
- "The telephone number is incomplete."
- "Select a service before submitting the form."

The W3C recommends providing instructions and feedback that help people complete forms successfully. Its [form instructions guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/instructions/) and [input validation guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/validation/) provide practical implementation advice.

A successful submission should also produce clear feedback. Visitors should not have to guess whether their enquiry was received.

See the W3C's [user notification guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/notifications/) for examples of accessible success and error feedback.

## 6. Make buttons and touch controls easier to use

A small icon may be visually attractive but difficult to activate accurately.

This is especially relevant on touchscreens, where visitors use their fingers rather than a precise mouse pointer.

Important controls should have enough space around them and should not be crowded together.

WCAG 2.2 includes a Level AA minimum target-size criterion of 24 by 24 CSS pixels, subject to specified exceptions. Its Level AAA enhanced criterion uses 44 by 44 CSS pixels.

These are not instructions to make every button exactly the same size. They provide measurable requirements and guidance for different circumstances.

For important actions such as submitting a form, opening navigation or calling a business, a larger and more comfortable target may be preferable.

Consider the following:

- Make primary buttons easy to identify.
- Leave sufficient space between adjacent controls.
- Avoid relying on tiny icon-only buttons.
- Provide accessible names for icon buttons.
- Keep important controls visible at mobile widths.
- Ensure menus can be opened and closed using supported input methods.

The [W3C explanation of target size](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum) explains why small, closely spaced controls can be difficult for some visitors to use.

## 7. Avoid unnecessary visual and interaction complexity

Animations, pop-ups, carousels and sticky elements can be useful, but they should not make the website harder to operate.

A promotional pop-up that covers the main content, a carousel that moves too quickly or a menu that opens only when a pointer hovers over it can create unnecessary barriers.

Ask whether each interactive feature serves a genuine purpose.

If a carousel is necessary, provide controls that are accessible to keyboard users and make its movement predictable. If a dialog opens, ensure focus is managed correctly and the visitor can close it without difficulty.

Do not make essential information dependent on animation or hover effects.

A straightforward interface is often easier to maintain and less likely to introduce unexpected accessibility problems.

## 8. Consider mobile accessibility and low-data conditions

Accessibility and mobile usability overlap.

A website may technically fit a mobile screen but still be difficult to use because its text is too small, controls are crowded or important content is hidden behind an awkward navigation menu.

Test the website at different viewport sizes and with enlarged text.

Also consider visitors using constrained mobile connections. Large background videos, unnecessary animations and excessive third-party scripts can delay the appearance of useful content.

The South African Government Communication and Information System includes mobile-first design and low-data optimisation among the practices recommended for government websites. Those guidelines are directed at government departments, not a universal legal requirement for every private business, but the usability considerations are relevant more broadly.

The [GCIS website accessibility guidance](https://www.gcis.gov.za/guidelines/website/website-accessibility) provides a useful South African reference.

## 9. Test accessibility as part of website maintenance

Accessibility should be reviewed during development and whenever significant content or functionality changes.

Automated accessibility tools can identify many issues, including missing labels, certain contrast problems and some structural errors. However, automated testing cannot reliably determine whether every page is understandable or whether a complete customer journey works for every user.

Combine automated checks with manual testing.

A practical review might include:

| Test | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| Keyboard | Can all important controls be reached and operated? |
| Focus | Is the current focus visible? |
| Headings | Do headings describe a logical content structure? |
| Images | Do informative images have meaningful alternatives? |
| Contrast | Is text distinguishable from its background? |
| Forms | Are labels, instructions and error messages clear? |
| Mobile | Can visitors use the page without awkward scrolling or tiny controls? |
| Zoom | Does content remain usable when text is enlarged? |
| Feedback | Are successful and unsuccessful actions communicated? |

Test the pages that matter most to the business first. A contact form, booking journey or quotation request deserves particular attention because an inaccessible control can prevent someone from completing an important task.

## 10. Is WCAG compliance legally required for every business?

WCAG is an internationally recognised technical standard, but its publication does not automatically make every criterion a legal requirement for every private website in every country.

The legal obligations applicable to a business depend on the relevant legislation, sector, contracts and circumstances.

South African government departments have specific published website guidance, including recommendations concerning WCAG. Private businesses should not assume that the GCIS guidance is a blanket legal rule for all commercial websites.

Nevertheless, accessibility is a worthwhile development objective. It can reduce avoidable usability barriers and make important services easier to access.

Businesses that have contractual, sector-specific or other accessibility obligations should obtain appropriate advice and assess the applicable requirements rather than relying on a general checklist.

## A practical accessibility improvement plan

A [small business](/articles/tag/small-business) does not need to rebuild its website immediately to begin improving accessibility.

Start with the most important customer journeys.

**First, review the content.** Check headings, links, images, instructions and readability.

**Second, test the interface.** Navigate the website using only a keyboard and check the focus indicator.

**Third, inspect the forms.** Confirm that every field has a label and that errors and success messages are understandable.

**Fourth, review mobile layouts.** Check text size, touch targets, spacing and navigation.

**Fifth, use automated tools.** Run an accessibility scan and investigate the issues it identifies.

**Finally, test again.** Repeat the same checks after changes and include accessibility in future development work.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does accessibility only help people with disabilities?

No. Clear navigation, readable text, understandable forms and predictable interactions can improve usability for many visitors, including people using older devices or smaller screens.

### Is adding alt text enough to make a website accessible?

No. Alt text is one part of accessibility. Keyboard navigation, contrast, headings, forms, captions and other requirements also need attention.

### Can an automated accessibility checker guarantee WCAG compliance?

No. Automated tools can identify useful issues, but manual testing and appropriate evaluation are also necessary.

### Should a small business aim for WCAG 2.2 Level AA?

WCAG 2.2 Level AA is a useful target for many website projects. The appropriate conformance objective should be considered in light of the business's obligations, audience and technical requirements.

## Conclusion

An accessible website is easier for more people to use.

Start with the fundamentals: clear structure, keyboard access, readable content, meaningful image alternatives, properly labelled forms and controls that are comfortable to operate.

These improvements do not need to happen all at once. By including accessibility in normal website development and maintenance, a business can avoid accumulating unnecessary barriers as its website grows.

The goal is simple: make it easier for every potential customer to understand the business and complete the actions the website was designed to support.

A website URL is more than an address that takes someone to a page.

It is part of the way visitors recognise a website, understand its content and decide whether a link looks relevant. It also helps search engines discover and interpret the pages that make up a website.

Yet [URL structure](/articles/tag/url-structure) is often treated as an afterthought.

A business might launch with short, readable page addresses, then gradually introduce inconsistent naming, unnecessary parameters, duplicate paths and confusing redirects as the website grows.

Eventually, even a relatively small website can become difficult to maintain.

[Google Search](/articles/tag/google-search) Central updated its URL structure documentation on 23 October 2026, clarifying its guidance on separating words with hyphens rather than underscores and on URL parameters.

This was a documentation clarification, not a new ranking algorithm announcement. The underlying recommendation is practical: make URLs understandable, consistent and easy for search engines to crawl.

For a [small business](/articles/tag/small-business), a sensible URL structure can make future content management, website migrations and SEO maintenance considerably easier.

## What makes a URL SEO-friendly?

An SEO-friendly URL is an address that is understandable, consistent and appropriate for the content it identifies.

Consider these two examples:

- `example.co.za/services/website-development/`
- `example.co.za/page.php?id=48271&section=9`

Both could lead to a working page, but the first gives visitors a clearer indication of what they are about to open.

Google's [URL structure best practices](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/url-structure) recommend using readable words rather than long, unclear identifiers where possible.

This does not mean that every URL needs to contain a complete page title or a collection of search keywords.

A URL should be useful first. It should help identify the page without becoming unnecessarily long or complicated.

## 1. Use descriptive words

A descriptive URL helps people understand the destination before opening it.

For example:

- `/services/website-development/`
- `/articles/business-record-keeping/`
- `/contact/`

These addresses are easier to interpret than automatically generated paths containing long numeric identifiers.

Descriptive URLs are especially useful when people share links through email, messaging applications, documents and social media.

A business owner should be able to recognise the general purpose of a link without having to open it.

However, descriptive does not mean excessively detailed.

A URL such as:

`/articles/best-affordable-professional-small-business-website-development-services-for-growing-companies/`

is unnecessarily long.

A shorter address such as:

`/articles/small-business-website-development/`

is easier to manage and still communicates the subject.

Aim for clarity rather than maximum keyword inclusion.

## 2. Use hyphens instead of underscores

One of Google's clarified recommendations is to use hyphens to separate words in URLs where possible.

For example:

**Recommended**

    /small-business-website/

**Not recommended**

    /small_business_website/

**Also avoid joining separate words**

    /smallbusinesswebsite/

Google explains that hyphens clearly indicate word boundaries, while underscores have historically been used in programming and other contexts to join concepts or identifiers.

The recommendation is documented in Google's [URL structure guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/url-structure).

The documentation update log records the clarification on 23 October 2026. You can follow the [Google Search Central documentation updates](https://developers.google.com/search/updates) for further changes.

Does this mean a business should immediately rename every existing URL containing an underscore?

No.

If an existing URL is working, has external links and is already indexed, changing it solely to replace underscores may introduce unnecessary migration work.

The better approach is to use hyphens consistently for new URLs and plan any necessary changes to existing addresses carefully.

## 3. Keep URLs in a consistent format

Consistency makes a website easier to manage.

Decide how the website will handle:

- Uppercase and lowercase letters.
- Trailing slashes.
- Word separators.
- Category paths.
- Article slugs.
- Product identifiers.
- Query parameters.

For example, these addresses may be treated as different URLs by a server or search engine:

- `/Services/Website-Development/`
- `/services/website-development/`

Google explains that URL handling is case-sensitive. If a website's server treats uppercase and lowercase paths as equivalent, the business should standardise them to reduce ambiguity.

A common approach is to use lowercase URLs throughout the website.

Trailing slash behaviour should also be consistent. Some [websites](/articles/tag/websites) use `/contact/`, while others use `/contact`. Either can work, but the website should avoid serving both versions as separate pages without a clear canonical arrangement.

Consistency is more important than choosing one particular style because it looks fashionable.

## 4. Organise URLs around the website's information structure

A website should have a logical structure that reflects its content.

For example, a small business website might use:

| Content type | Example URL |
| --- | --- |
| Main service | `/services/website-development/` |
| Another service | `/services/search-engine-optimisation/` |
| Article | `/articles/website-backup-testing/` |
| Promotion | `/promotions/website-package/` |
| Contact page | `/contact/` |

The structure should help visitors and website administrators understand where information belongs.

Avoid creating deep URL hierarchies simply because the [CMS](/articles/tag/cms) allows them.

A path such as:

`/business/services/digital/online/website/development/basic/`

may be more complicated than necessary if the website has no meaningful reason for each level.

A shorter structure can be easier to maintain:

`/services/website-development/`

The hierarchy should reflect a genuine organisational relationship rather than an attempt to insert more keywords.

## 5. Use the language your audience understands

Google recommends using words in the language of the intended audience.

This is important for businesses serving multilingual communities.

A business that communicates with customers in English, Setswana, isiZulu or another language should consider whether the page address remains understandable to the people it is intended to serve.

Do not mix languages randomly within a URL simply to include additional search terms.

Choose a consistent approach that reflects the website's content and audience.

If a business serves customers in [Maboloka](/locations/maboloka), [Soshanguve](/locations/soshanguve), [Centurion](/locations/centurion) or surrounding areas, its URL structure should still be based on useful content and clear information architecture.

Adding a place name to a URL does not automatically make a page valuable or relevant. The page itself must provide a genuine reason for existing.

## 6. Avoid unnecessary URL parameters

URL parameters are the values that appear after a question mark in an address.

For example:

    /products?category=shoes&sort=price

Parameters can be useful. They allow websites to filter information, sort results and pass data between systems.

Problems arise when a website creates large numbers of URLs that display substantially the same content.

Consider a product catalogue with filters for:

- Colour.
- Size.
- Brand.
- Price.
- Availability.
- Sorting order.

If visitors can combine every filter in many different ways, the website may generate a very large number of URLs.

Some of those addresses may show nearly identical lists of products.

Google explains that excessive URL variations can create crawling inefficiencies and make it harder for search engines to discover the content that matters.

Its [URL structure documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/url-structure) discusses additive filters, irrelevant parameters and session identifiers as potential sources of unnecessary URL complexity.

Review parameters that do not change the actual content.

Examples may include:

- Tracking identifiers.
- Unnecessary referral values.
- Session IDs.
- Duplicate sorting parameters.
- Repeated filter combinations.

Where possible, keep the number of indexable URL variations under control.

Do not remove parameters that are essential to the website's functionality. The objective is to prevent unnecessary URL duplication, not to break the application.

## 7. Do not use URL fragments as separate content pages

A URL fragment is the part of an address that follows a hash symbol.

For example:

    example.co.za/#contact

Fragments are useful for linking to a section of a page.

They can also be used by JavaScript applications to manage certain types of navigation.

However, Google generally does not support URL fragments as a way of identifying separate content pages.

If a business website uses:

- `example.co.za/#services`
- `example.co.za/#about`
- `example.co.za/#contact`

to display entirely different content without proper page URLs, it may be making its content structure harder to understand.

For separate indexable pages, use actual paths such as:

- `/services/`
- `/about/`
- `/contact/`

Google's documentation recommends using the History API rather than fragments when JavaScript changes the content of a page in a way that requires separate URL handling.

This is especially relevant when a website uses a single-page application architecture.

## 8. Understand canonical URLs

Sometimes the same or very similar content can be accessed through more than one URL.

For example:

- `/services/website-development/`
- `/services/website-development/?source=newsletter`
- `/Services/Website-Development/`

Depending on the server and application configuration, these may create duplicate or near-duplicate versions of the same content.

A canonical URL tells search engines which version the website considers preferred.

A canonical link may look like this:

    <link rel="canonical" href="https://example.co.za/services/website-development/" />

Google describes redirects, canonical link annotations and sitemap inclusion as signals that can help establish preferred URLs.

Its [canonical URL guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls) explains how these methods work and why they should be used consistently.

Important points include:

- Use a self-referencing canonical on the preferred page.
- Link internally to the preferred URL.
- Keep sitemap entries consistent with the canonical URLs.
- Avoid declaring different canonical destinations for the same content.
- Do not use `robots.txt` as a canonicalisation method.

A canonical tag is not a replacement for every redirect. If an old URL has genuinely been retired, a permanent redirect may be more appropriate.

## 9. Do not change existing URLs casually

One of the most expensive URL mistakes is changing addresses without planning what happens to the old ones.

Imagine that a business has published articles for several years.

Some articles may have external links, bookmarks, social shares and existing search visibility.

If the business changes its URL structure during a redesign and does not redirect the old addresses, visitors may encounter errors.

Search engines may also need to discover and process the new URLs.

A URL migration should therefore be treated as a technical project rather than a cosmetic cleanup.

Google's [site migration guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/site-move-with-url-changes) recommends preparing a URL mapping, configuring redirects, updating internal links and monitoring the old and new URLs.

A practical migration process follows.

### Step 1: List existing URLs

Gather the important URLs from:

- Current XML sitemaps.
- Search Console.
- Website analytics.
- Internal navigation.
- External links.
- CMS exports.
- Server logs, where available.

Include important documents and media files if their URLs will change.

### Step 2: Map each old URL to its new destination

Create a table that records the old address and the corresponding new address.

| Old URL | New URL | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/old-services/` | `/services/` | Permanent redirect |
| `/website-design.html` | `/services/website-development/` | Permanent redirect |
| `/old-article/` | `/articles/new-article/` | Permanent redirect |
| `/retired-page/` | None | Return an appropriate 404 or 410 |

Do not redirect every deleted page to the homepage.

A redirect should lead to a relevant replacement. Redirecting unrelated pages to a generic destination can confuse visitors and may be treated as a soft 404.

### Step 3: Implement permanent redirects

Where a page has moved permanently, use an appropriate server-side permanent redirect.

Common examples include HTTP 301 and 308 redirects.

Avoid unnecessary redirect chains.

For example, instead of:

`/old-page/` → `/new-page/` → `/final-page/`

redirect the old URL directly to the final destination.

### Step 4: Update internal links

Internal links should point directly to the new URLs.

Do not rely on redirects for every internal navigation link when the website owner can update the links themselves.

Update:

- Navigation menus.
- Footer links.
- Article references.
- Related-content links.
- Breadcrumbs.
- Sitemap entries.
- Canonical annotations.

### Step 5: Monitor the migration

Use Search Console to monitor indexing and inspect important URLs.

Check whether:

- New URLs are accessible.
- Old URLs redirect correctly.
- Important pages return the expected status codes.
- Canonical annotations point to the correct destinations.
- The new sitemap contains the intended URLs.
- Visitors are still reaching important pages.

Google recommends keeping redirects in place for as long as possible and generally for at least one year after a site move.

## 10. Build URLs with future growth in mind

A website's structure should be able to accommodate new content without requiring repeated restructuring.

A small business might begin with five pages and later add:

- New services.
- Case studies.
- Articles.
- Promotions.
- Product categories.
- Customer resources.
- Downloadable documents.

Before launching a new section, decide where it belongs and how its URL should be constructed.

Avoid creating new paths based on temporary campaign names or internal project identifiers unless there is a clear reason.

For example, a campaign page might initially be published at:

`/campaign-november-2026/`

If the content is intended to remain useful after the campaign ends, a more durable URL may be appropriate.

A stable URL makes it easier to keep links working as the website evolves.

## 11. Create a URL naming standard

A short internal standard can prevent inconsistencies when several people publish or maintain website content.

The standard could specify:

- Lowercase letters.
- Hyphens between words.
- Short descriptive slugs.
- No unnecessary dates.
- No internal database IDs in public-facing paths.
- Consistent trailing slash behaviour.
- A clear hierarchy for articles and services.
- A review process before changing existing URLs.

It should also define who approves URL changes.

If a content editor can change a published article's slug without understanding redirects, the website may accumulate broken links over time.

A simple approval step can prevent unnecessary changes.

> **SEO audit:**

> If you want to identify URL duplication, indexing problems and [technical SEO](/articles/tag/technical-seo) issues on your website, explore the [Mogen SEO audit](/services/seo/#audit).

## SEO-friendly URL checklist

Use this checklist when publishing new pages or reviewing an existing website:

- [ ] The URL describes the page clearly.
- [ ] Words are separated with hyphens.
- [ ] The URL uses a consistent case format.
- [ ] The path is not unnecessarily long.
- [ ] The URL reflects the website's information structure.
- [ ] The audience can understand the words used.
- [ ] Unnecessary parameters have been removed where appropriate.
- [ ] Duplicate versions have a clear canonical arrangement.
- [ ] Internal links use the preferred URL.
- [ ] Important pages appear in the sitemap.
- [ ] Existing URLs are mapped before migration.
- [ ] Permanent redirects lead to relevant destinations.
- [ ] Redirect chains and broken links are checked.
- [ ] Search Console is monitored after changes.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do hyphens improve Google rankings?

Google recommends hyphens because they make word boundaries clearer to users and search engines. This should not be interpreted as a guaranteed ranking improvement or a reason to rename every existing URL.

### Are underscores bad for SEO?

Google does not recommend underscores as word separators when creating URLs. Existing pages that use underscores do not automatically need to be changed. Consider the value and risk of a migration before altering established URLs.

### Should every URL contain my primary keyword?

No. A URL should describe the page naturally. Repeating keywords or creating excessively long addresses does not make a website more useful.

### Is a canonical tag the same as a redirect?

No. A canonical tag indicates a preferred version of similar or duplicate content, while a redirect sends a visitor and crawler from one URL to another. They solve related but different problems.

### Will changing my URLs cause my rankings to drop?

A migration can cause temporary search visibility fluctuations while search engines process the changes. Poorly implemented redirects, missing pages and inconsistent canonical signals can create additional problems. Planning and monitoring reduce avoidable risks.

### Should a small business use short URLs?

Short URLs are often easier to share and maintain, but clarity matters more than an arbitrary character limit. Use enough descriptive words to identify the page without unnecessary detail.

> **SEO planning:**
>
> Visit the [Mogen promotions page](/promotions) to review currently published offers before planning improvements to your website's search visibility.

## Conclusion

Good URL structure is not about inserting as many keywords as possible into a web address.

It is about creating a consistent system that visitors can understand and that the website can maintain as it grows.

Google's October 2026 clarification reinforces useful fundamentals: use readable words, separate them with hyphens, avoid unnecessary parameters and keep the URL structure manageable.

For businesses planning a redesign or migration, the most important decision is to protect existing URLs and map changes carefully.

A well-planned URL structure can support better website organisation, more reliable navigation and a cleaner technical foundation for ongoing SEO work.
