--- title: "Make Your Website Images Search-Ready" slug: "make-website-images-search-ready" description: "Help Google discover and understand your website images with descriptive filenames, useful alt text, responsive files and relevant page context." publishedAt: "2026-11-02" updatedAt: "2026-11-02" author: "Mogen" category: "SEO" type: "evergreen" primaryKeyword: "image SEO" secondaryKeywords: - "Google Images optimisation" - "image alt text SEO" - "image file naming" - "responsive images" - "image sitemap" - "website image optimisation" tags: - "SEO" - "image SEO" - "technical SEO" - "website content" - "Google Images" - "search visibility" - "accessibility" - "websites" featured: false heroImage: "/images/articles/modern-seo-workspace-1.png" heroImageAlt: "Modern Seo Workspace" --- Images can help a business website explain its services, demonstrate products and give visitors confidence in what the organisation offers. They can also create additional opportunities for discovery through [Google Images](/articles/tag/google-images) and other visual search experiences. However, uploading photographs to a website is not the same as optimising them for search. A photograph with an automatically generated filename, no useful alternative text and little connection to the surrounding page gives search engines limited context about what it represents. The same image may also be unnecessarily large, slowing down the page for visitors using mobile data. [Image SEO](/articles/tag/image-seo) brings together several disciplines: [search visibility](/articles/tag/search-visibility), [accessibility](/articles/tag/accessibility), content relevance and technical performance. Google's current [image SEO best-practice documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/google-images) explains how website owners can help Google discover, understand and index their images. For small and growing South African businesses, improving image SEO can make existing [website content](/articles/tag/website-content) more useful without requiring a completely new marketing strategy. ## Why image SEO matters Google offers several ways for people to discover visual content, including Google Images, images associated with ordinary search results and Google Discover. These experiences can help users find: - Products. - Business locations. - Service examples. - Portfolio work. - Educational diagrams. - Instructional photographs. - Informational content. A business that sells furniture, for example, should not rely entirely on text to explain its products. Clear product photographs can help visitors understand the design, finish, size and appearance of an item. A construction business may use project photographs to demonstrate the type of work it has completed. A professional services firm may use original diagrams to explain complicated processes. Images can therefore support both the visitor's decision-making process and the wider content of a website. However, appearing in Google Images is not guaranteed. Optimisation improves discoverability and context; it does not promise a particular ranking or volume of traffic. ## 1. Use descriptive image filenames One of the easiest improvements is to replace generic image filenames with meaningful descriptions. Consider these examples: **Generic filename** ```text IMG_20261102_0045.jpg ``` **Descriptive filename** ```text wooden-office-desk-custom-cabinet.jpg ``` The second filename gives a clearer indication of what the image contains. Google explains that filenames provide lightweight clues about image subject matter. Its documentation recommends short, descriptive filenames rather than generic identifiers such as `image1.jpg` or `pic.gif`. A useful filename should: - Describe the actual image. - Use a small number of relevant words. - Separate words with hyphens. - Avoid unnecessary dates and identifiers. - Avoid repeating the same keyword excessively. - Remain understandable to someone viewing the filename. Do not turn the filename into a list of search phrases. For example: ```text cheap-web-design-websites-web-design-south-africa-websites.jpg ``` is not a useful description. A more natural filename would be: ```text small-business-website-homepage-design.jpg ``` The purpose is to identify the image, not to force additional keywords into its address. ## 2. Write useful alternative text Alternative text, usually called alt text, describes an image when it cannot be seen or when assistive technology needs to communicate its content. It is important for accessibility and can also help search engines understand what an image represents. Consider a photograph showing a carpenter fitting a wooden kitchen cabinet. A useful alt description could be: ```text Carpenter fitting a wooden kitchen cabinet in a residential kitchen. ``` This describes the actual image in a natural way. Compare it with: ```text Kitchen cupboards carpenter cabinets kitchen renovations kitchen design cheap carpenter near me. ``` The second example is keyword stuffing rather than useful image description. Google's guidance specifically warns against filling alt attributes with keywords because this creates a poor experience and may be treated as spam. ### Alt text should describe the image's purpose The right description depends on why the image appears on the page. If a photograph demonstrates a completed project, describe what is visible. If an image contains a chart, explain the information that the chart communicates. Where the chart contains detailed data, provide an equivalent explanation in the surrounding page content. If an image is used as a link, the alternative text should help communicate the destination or purpose of the link. If an image is purely decorative, an empty alt attribute may be appropriate: ```text alt="" ``` This prevents assistive technology from announcing decorative content that adds no meaningful information. ### Do not repeat the surrounding heading Alt text should add useful context rather than repeat the page title word for word. If the heading already explains that a page is about website development, an image of a laptop showing a website preview could have a more specific description. The objective is to describe what the visitor would miss if the image were unavailable. ## 3. Place images near relevant content An image should appear in a section that explains or discusses the subject it represents. Imagine an article about kitchen renovations that includes: - A photograph of a completed kitchen. - A diagram showing cabinet measurements. - An image explaining countertop materials. Each image should appear near the text that discusses it. This creates a clearer relationship between the image and the page's subject. Google's documentation explains that the content of the page, captions, image titles and surrounding text can help its systems understand an image. Avoid placing unrelated stock photographs throughout a page simply to make it appear more visually interesting. A relevant image is more useful to the visitor and provides better context for search engines. ## 4. Use original photographs where possible Original images can help a business communicate its actual products, people, services and work. For example: - A furniture manufacturer can photograph its own products. - A restaurant can show its actual dishes and dining environment. - A contractor can display completed projects with the customer's permission. - A consultant can create original diagrams explaining a process. - A training provider can show genuine training environments. Stock photography may still be useful for general illustrations, but it should not create a misleading impression about the business. If a business serves customers in [Maboloka](/locations/maboloka), [Soshanguve](/locations/soshanguve), [Centurion](/locations/centurion) or surrounding areas, photographs should accurately represent the business, its work or its premises. Do not use a photograph of a building, office or project in a particular location if the business has no legitimate connection to it. Do not present generated images as photographs of completed customer projects. Authentic visual evidence can help customers understand what the business actually provides. ## 5. Optimise image dimensions and file sizes A photograph may look perfectly reasonable on a desktop screen but be unnecessarily large for a mobile device. A common mistake is uploading a high-resolution photograph directly from a camera and displaying the original file at a much smaller size. This can force mobile visitors to download more data than the page requires. Google's image documentation recommends applying modern image optimisation and responsive image techniques because images can contribute significantly to overall page size. The [web.dev image performance guide](https://web.dev/learn/performance/image-performance) explains that images are often among the heaviest resources on a website and that serving appropriately sized files can reduce the number of bytes transferred. Practical improvements include: - Resize photographs to suit their display dimensions. - Compress images while maintaining acceptable visual quality. - Use modern formats such as WebP or AVIF where appropriate. - Avoid uploading several unnecessary versions of the same photograph. - Generate smaller image variants for narrower screens. - Preserve a suitable fallback for browsers that do not support a selected format. There is no universal file-size target that works for every image. A small thumbnail and a full-width project photograph have different requirements. The correct balance is to deliver enough detail for the intended use without making visitors download unnecessary data. ## 6. Use responsive images Responsive images allow the browser to select an appropriate image file for the available screen space and device characteristics. For example, a desktop screen may display a large photograph while a mobile device only needs a smaller version. Instead of forcing every visitor to download the largest file, developers can provide multiple versions using the HTML `srcset` and `sizes` attributes. A simplified example is: ```text ``` The browser uses the available information to choose an appropriate file. The [MDN responsive images guide](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Guides/Responsive_images) explains how `srcset`, `sizes` and the `picture` element support different image sizes and display requirements. Responsive image implementation is particularly useful for [websites](/articles/tag/websites) with large product catalogues, image galleries and project portfolios. ## 7. Use standard HTML image elements for important content There is a technical distinction between an image embedded in HTML and an image used purely as a CSS background. Google explains that its systems can discover images through the `src` attribute of an HTML `img` element. Google does not index CSS background images in the same way. For important content images, use an appropriate HTML image element. For example: ```text ``` CSS background images are still useful for decorative elements, visual treatments and backgrounds. They should not be the only way important visual information is made available. This distinction is especially important when the image itself communicates something meaningful about a product, service or article. ## 8. Add appropriate image dimensions Images should have suitable width and height attributes where practical. These values help the browser reserve space for the image before the file has finished loading. Without reserved space, page elements may move when the image appears. This can create an unstable experience, especially when several images load as someone scrolls through a long article or gallery. For example: ```text ``` The dimensions should reflect the actual image's aspect ratio. Do not insert arbitrary dimensions simply to make the code appear complete. ## 9. Use lazy loading carefully Lazy loading delays the retrieval of images that are not immediately needed. It can reduce unnecessary network usage when a page contains many images below the initial viewport. For example, an article with ten photographs does not necessarily need to download all ten before the visitor can begin reading. An image further down the page can use: ```text loading="lazy" ``` However, avoid applying lazy loading indiscriminately. The main hero image or another important image visible immediately when the page opens should normally be loaded promptly. Delaying the main visible image can make the page appear slower. A sensible strategy is to load important above-the-fold images eagerly and defer non-critical images lower down the page. ## 10. Create an image sitemap when useful An XML image sitemap can provide search engines with additional information about images on a website. It can be particularly useful when a website has a large number of images or when important image URLs are not easily discovered through ordinary crawling. Google explains that image sitemaps can help it discover images that might otherwise be difficult to find. An image sitemap is not compulsory for every small website. Before creating one, confirm that: - Important images are already accessible. - The image URLs return successful responses. - The pages containing those images can be crawled. - The sitemap references the correct image locations. - CDN-hosted images are configured appropriately. - The sitemap does not contain obsolete or broken files. A sitemap is a discovery aid, not a guarantee that every submitted image will be indexed. ## 11. Provide appropriate image metadata Images used in search previews and social sharing should be selected carefully. Google's documentation explains that website owners can provide preferred image information through metadata such as: - Schema.org `primaryImageOfPage`. - The `image` property associated with a main entity. - The Open Graph `og:image` property. For an article, the selected image should represent the article rather than simply repeat the website logo. Use a suitable image with enough resolution for the intended preview. Avoid extremely narrow or unusually wide images when choosing a primary image for search or sharing metadata. Structured data can make content eligible for certain search features, but it does not guarantee that Google will display a particular image or rich result. ## 12. Make image optimisation part of the publishing process Image SEO should not be a task that happens only when a website receives an audit. It should form part of the content-publishing workflow. Before publishing a new article, product or service page, check the images being added. | Check | What to verify | | --- | --- | | Filename | Descriptive and understandable | | Alt text | Accurate and useful | | Relevance | Image supports the surrounding content | | Dimensions | Appropriate for the display size | | File size | Compressed without unacceptable quality loss | | Format | Suitable for the image and browser support | | Responsive behaviour | Smaller files available where appropriate | | Loading | Important images are not unnecessarily delayed | | Metadata | Preferred image information is accurate | | Licensing | Business has permission to use the image | A consistent process helps prevent image quality, accessibility and performance problems from accumulating as the website grows. > **SEO audit:** > > If your website contains many images or you are unsure how well its content is being discovered, explore the [Mogen SEO audit](/services/seo/#audit). ## How to measure image SEO performance Image optimisation should be evaluated using more than the number of photographs uploaded. Useful checks include: **Google Search Console** Review the Search performance report and select the Image search type where available. Examine impressions, clicks, click-through rate and the queries associated with image discovery. Look for pages and images that receive visibility but attract limited engagement. **Page performance** Use PageSpeed Insights and browser developer tools to identify oversized images, unnecessary downloads and image-loading issues. **Accessibility** Review whether meaningful images have useful alternative text and whether decorative images are handled appropriately. **Business outcomes** If image traffic reaches product or service pages, assess whether visitors proceed to enquiries, purchases or other meaningful actions. A photograph that attracts search traffic but does not help visitors understand the business may not be contributing much commercial value. ## Frequently asked questions ### Does image SEO improve Google rankings? Image SEO helps search engines discover and understand visual content. It can create opportunities for image search visibility, but it does not guarantee higher rankings for the page or image. ### Should every image have alt text? Meaningful content images should have appropriate alternative text. Decorative images can use an empty alt attribute so that assistive technology does not announce unnecessary information. ### Are image filenames important? Descriptive filenames provide additional context about an image. They are useful, but they are only one of several signals that search engines can consider. ### Should I use WebP or AVIF? Both are modern image formats that can reduce file sizes compared with some traditional formats. Choose a format that suits the image, browser support and delivery requirements, and provide appropriate fallbacks where necessary. ### Do I need an image sitemap? Not every website needs a separate image sitemap. It can be helpful for larger sites or where important images are difficult for search engines to discover. ### Can I use stock photographs? Yes, where the business has the appropriate licence. However, stock photographs should not misrepresent the business, its staff, premises or completed work. > **SEO planning:** > > Visit the [Mogen promotions page](/promotions) to review currently published offers before planning improvements to your website's search visibility. ## Conclusion Images are part of the content and technical structure of a website. They help visitors understand products and services, provide visual evidence and create additional opportunities for discovery through search. The most useful image SEO improvements are straightforward: use descriptive filenames, write meaningful alt text, place images in relevant content, serve appropriately sized files and ensure important images are accessible to search engines. These practices also improve accessibility and can reduce unnecessary data usage. For a growing business, image optimisation should become a normal part of publishing rather than an afterthought. ## Sources - [Google Search Central: Google Image SEO Best Practices](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/google-images) - [MDN: Using Responsive Images in HTML](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Guides/Responsive_images) - [web.dev: Image Performance](https://web.dev/learn/performance/image-performance)

  A business can rank for a keyword and still receive few useful enquiries. It can also improve the visibility of several service pages without immediately seeing a corresponding increase in sales.

  This is why keyword positions alone do not provide a complete picture of search engine optimisation ([SEO](/services/seo)).

  Rankings are useful diagnostic information, but business owners also need to understand whether the right people are discovering their services, visiting relevant pages and taking meaningful action.

  For businesses serving [Maboloka](/locations/maboloka), [Soshanguve](/locations/soshanguve), [Centurion](/locations/centurion) and surrounding areas, measurement should connect search visibility with genuine business outcomes. The objective is not simply to appear in search results. It is to become easier for appropriate customers to discover and evaluate the business.

  ## 1. Start with the business objective

  Before opening a report, define what SEO should help the business achieve.

  Possible objectives include:
  - Generating relevant quotation requests.
  - Increasing enquiries for a particular service.
  - Helping customers discover a product catalogue.
  - Improving visibility for a genuine service area.
  - Increasing qualified visits to important pages.
  - Supporting online sales or appointment bookings.

  These objectives require different measures.

  A business that relies on telephone enquiries may care about qualified calls. An online shop may focus on completed purchases. A consultancy may prioritise relevant enquiries rather than the total number of visitors.

  Decide what success means before selecting the metrics.

  ## 2. Understand what Google Search Console measures

  Google [Search Console](/articles/tag/search-console) provides information about how a website performs in Google Search.

  Its official [Search results Performance report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7576553?hl=en) includes metrics such as clicks, impressions, click-through rate and average position. Data can be grouped by queries, pages, countries, devices and other dimensions.

  These measures answer different questions.

  ### Impressions

  An impression indicates that a result from your website appeared in Google Search under the reporting system's counting rules.

  Impressions can help identify whether pages are becoming visible for relevant queries. However, more impressions do not automatically mean more interested customers.

  A page may receive impressions for searches that are only loosely connected to the business.

  Review the queries and pages responsible for the change before deciding whether it represents a useful opportunity.

  ### Clicks

  Clicks show how often people selected your website from Google Search results.

  Relevant clicks can indicate that your pages are attracting searchers. But total clicks alone do not reveal whether visitors found the right information or became customers.

  Examine the pages receiving clicks and consider whether they match the services the business wants to promote.

  ### Click-through rate

  Click-through rate (CTR) is the number of clicks divided by impressions.

  CTR can help identify pages whose search appearances attract relatively few clicks. Before changing a title or description, inspect the queries, search result format, position and competing results.

  A low CTR does not prove that a title is poorly written. The page may appear for a broad query, be shown in a different search feature or receive impressions from people whose needs do not match the offer.

  ### Average position

  Average position summarises the position of the website's results under Google's reporting methodology.

  It is useful for examining broad trends, but it is not a promise that every searcher will see the same ranking. Google notes that search results vary according to factors such as the searcher's location, device and search context.

  A business serving Centurion should therefore avoid treating a single manual search as a definitive measurement of visibility for every customer in the area.

  ## 3. Separate visibility from business performance

  Search Console measures search performance. It does not, by itself, tell you how many enquiries became paying customers.

  A practical reporting process connects several stages:

  1. **Visibility:** Are relevant pages appearing for appropriate searches?
  2. **Visits:** Are people clicking through to those pages?
  3. **Engagement:** Are visitors finding useful information and using the intended contact routes?
  4. **Enquiries:** Are relevant people contacting the business?
  5. **Commercial outcomes:** Are enquiries becoming quotations, bookings, sales or repeat business?

  Each stage can reveal a different problem.

  If visibility improves but clicks do not, review query relevance and search appearances. If clicks improve but enquiries remain low, inspect the landing page, service offer, contact process and audience fit.

  If enquiries increase but sales do not, the issue may involve pricing, response times, lead quality or the sales process rather than search visibility alone.

  SEO is only one part of the customer journey.

  ## 4. Measure the pages that matter most

  A site-wide total can hide important differences between pages.

  Separate your reporting by page purpose. For example:

  | Page type | What to investigate |
  |---|---|
  | Main service page | Relevant queries, visits and qualified enquiries |
  | Location-related page | Whether the content accurately reflects actual service coverage |
  | Educational article | Relevant discovery, onward visits and useful engagement |
  | Contact page | Whether visitors can complete the intended contact action |
  | Product or package page | Visits from suitable customers and resulting enquiries or sales |
  | Campaign landing page | Whether the page supports the campaign's specific objective |

  This makes it easier to identify where improvement work is likely to have value.

  A page that attracts fewer visitors may still be commercially important if it generates high-quality enquiries. Conversely, a popular article may have limited immediate commercial value while still helping people understand the business.

  Evaluate pages in context rather than ranking them only by traffic.

  ## 5. Connect SEO reporting with enquiry records

  Small businesses do not necessarily need a complicated [analytics](/articles/tag/analytics) system to begin measuring outcomes.

  A consistent enquiry register can record:
  - The date of the enquiry.
  - The service requested.
  - The customer's location, when relevant and appropriately collected.
  - How the enquiry was attributed, if known.
  - Whether it was relevant to the business.
  - Whether a quotation or booking followed.
  - The eventual outcome.

  Keep the information proportionate to the business purpose and protect personal information appropriately.

  If a customer says they found the business through Google, record that information where useful. This will not provide perfect attribution, but it can add context to website reporting.

  Where analytics or conversion tracking is implemented, test that it records the intended action correctly. A form submission event should not fire merely because someone opens the contact page.

  Avoid counting the same enquiry several times across multiple systems.

  ## 6. Use local reporting carefully

  Businesses serving Maboloka, Soshanguve, Centurion and surrounding areas may want to understand which locations generate relevant enquiries.

  That can be useful, but location reporting needs careful interpretation.

  A page mentioning a town does not prove that the business is visible for all searches in that town. Nor does a website visit from a particular location prove that the visitor is a suitable customer.

  Use location information where it is available and meaningful. Combine it with actual service capacity and enquiry quality.

  If the business does not serve a particular area, attracting more visitors from that area may not be a useful outcome.

  For eligible local businesses, Google Business Profile provides additional performance information. Website Search Console data and Business Profile data describe different aspects of discovery and should not be treated as identical measurements.

  ## 7. Investigate changes before drawing conclusions

  SEO performance can change for many reasons, including seasonality, competitor activity, website changes, changing customer demand and changes in how search results are displayed.

  A decline in clicks does not automatically mean that the website has been penalised. An increase does not necessarily mean that every recent SEO task succeeded.

  When a meaningful change appears:

  1. Confirm the reporting period and comparison dates.
  2. Check whether the change affects the whole site or particular pages.
  3. Inspect queries, devices and relevant page groups.
  4. Review recent website changes and technical issues.
  5. Compare the data with enquiry and sales records.
  6. Decide whether further investigation or a controlled improvement is justified.

  Do not make several unrelated changes at once if you need to understand which change affected the outcome.

  ## 8. Do not confuse more content with better SEO

  Publishing more pages can create more opportunities to answer customer questions, but volume alone is not a useful performance measure.

  Google's [people-first content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks creators to consider whether content provides original value, demonstrates appropriate knowledge and satisfies the needs of its intended audience. It also cautions against producing large amounts of content primarily to attract search traffic.

  For a business serving Maboloka or Soshanguve, one genuinely useful service page may be more valuable than several near-identical location pages.

  The same applies to articles. A practical explanation that helps a customer make a decision is more useful than a page that repeats a keyword without adding meaningful information.

  Review existing content as well as planning new content. Improving an important page may be a better use of time than publishing another article on a subject the website already covers adequately.

  ## 9. Create a simple monthly SEO report

  A report should help the business make decisions. It does not need dozens of charts.

  Start with a concise summary:

  | Reporting area | Question to answer |
  |---|---|
  | Search visibility | Are relevant pages appearing more or less often? |
  | Organic clicks | Are searchers visiting the website? |
  | Important pages | Which service pages or articles changed most? |
  | Technical issues | Are there indexing, usability or performance problems requiring attention? |
  | Enquiries | How many relevant enquiries were received, where this can be measured? |
  | Lead quality | Were the enquiries appropriate for the business? |
  | Actions | What should be improved next, and why? |

  Include the reporting period and the comparison period. Explain unusual changes and distinguish observations from assumptions.

  A useful report might say that impressions increased for a service page but qualified enquiries remained unchanged. The next step could be to inspect the queries, page content and contact journey.

  That is more actionable than simply reporting that rankings improved.

  ## Frequently asked questions

  ### Are keyword rankings still useful?

  Yes. Rankings can help diagnose visibility changes and understand how pages perform for relevant searches. They should be considered alongside clicks, query relevance, enquiries and business outcomes.

  ### How often should a small business review SEO?

  A monthly review is a practical starting point for many small businesses. Important technical issues may require more frequent monitoring, while short-term ranking fluctuations should not automatically trigger major changes.

  ### Why did traffic increase without more enquiries?

  The additional visits may not match the target audience, or the landing pages may not make the next step clear. Review query relevance, service information, contact options and enquiry tracking before assuming that more traffic is necessarily better.

  ### Can I measure SEO without expensive tools?

  Yes. Google Search Console provides useful search performance data, and a simple enquiry register can add business context. More advanced analytics may help later if the business has clear requirements and can maintain them properly.

  ## Conclusion

  Measuring SEO properly means connecting search visibility with the needs of the business.

  Search Console helps explain how pages appear and attract clicks. Enquiry records and conversion measurement help determine whether that visibility is contributing to meaningful outcomes.

  For businesses serving Maboloka, Soshanguve, Centurion and surrounding areas, the priority should be relevant discovery and qualified enquiries, not rankings for their own sake.

For many customers, a phone is the first place they encounter a business online. They may be comparing service providers, checking a price, reading reviews or trying to contact a company while away from a computer.

That makes mobile usability a business requirement, not merely a design preference.

Whether a business serves [Maboloka](/locations/maboloka), [Soshanguve](/locations/soshanguve), [Centurion](/locations/centurion) or surrounding areas, a mobile-first website should make essential information easy to find, load reliably and help visitors take the next step.

## What does mobile-first development mean?

Mobile-first development begins by designing for the constraints of a smaller screen and then progressively adapting the experience for larger displays. It encourages developers to prioritise essential content, straightforward navigation and efficient performance.

It does not mean that desktop users are unimportant. It means that the core experience should work well before additional space and capabilities are used to enhance it.

The South African Government Communication and Information System highlights responsive design, media optimisation, caching and low-bandwidth performance in its [website content-management guidance](https://www.gcis.gov.za/guidelines/website/cms).

## 1. Check the layout on real devices

A responsive layout should adapt to different screen widths without forcing users to zoom or scroll horizontally.

Test:
- Common phone screen sizes and orientations.
- Tablet and desktop layouts.
- Long headings and paragraphs.
- Navigation menus and dropdowns.
- Tables, images and embedded media.
- Forms and buttons near the bottom of the page.

Do not rely exclusively on a browser's device simulator. Test important journeys on actual phones where possible.

## 2. Make navigation simple

Mobile visitors should not have to guess where to find services or contact details.

Use descriptive menu labels, keep the most important destinations easy to reach, and avoid placing every page in the primary navigation. A clear hierarchy is better than a crowded menu.

A customer looking for a quotation should be able to identify the relevant service and contact option without navigating through several unrelated sections.

## 3. Keep pages lightweight

Slow pages can interrupt the customer journey, particularly when the connection is unreliable or the visitor has limited data.

Improve performance by:
- Resizing images before delivery.
- Using suitable modern image formats.
- Avoiding autoplay video backgrounds.
- Removing unnecessary third-party scripts.
- Loading below-the-fold media when needed.
- Using caching and efficient hosting configuration.
- Reviewing the impact of plugins and external widgets.

Measure the website before and after changes. A performance improvement should be verified rather than assumed.

> **Need a website built around your business?** Explore Mogen's [Sprout promotion](/promotions/mogen-sprout-first-100) to learn more about the business and its services.

## 4. Prioritise readable content

Mobile layouts need readable text, sufficient spacing and a clear visual hierarchy.

Use headings that describe the section, short paragraphs where appropriate and lists for steps or features. Ensure that buttons, links and form fields are easy to identify.

Avoid placing text over busy photographs unless contrast and readability remain reliable. Do not communicate important information through colour alone.

## 5. Make contact actions easy

Depending on the business, useful mobile actions may include calling, sending an email, opening WhatsApp or completing a short enquiry form.

Make sure each action works on a phone. Telephone numbers should use appropriate links, forms should have visible labels, and errors should explain how to correct a problem.

Keep forms proportionate to the enquiry. Asking for excessive personal information can discourage visitors and create unnecessary data-handling responsibilities.

## 6. Check accessibility

[Accessibility](/articles/tag/accessibility) improves the experience for people who use assistive technology or encounter visual, motor or cognitive barriers.

Include:
- Semantic headings and page structure.
- Keyboard-accessible navigation.
- Visible focus indicators.
- Sufficient colour contrast.
- Useful alternative text for meaningful images.
- Labels and instructions for form fields.
- Clear error messages.
- Captions or transcripts where appropriate.

The [GCIS accessibility guidance](https://www.gcis.gov.za/guidelines/website/website-accessibility) discusses WCAG and practical website accessibility considerations.

## 7. Test the complete customer journey

A page can look good while its most important function is broken.

Test the journey from arrival to completion:
1. Open a relevant service page.
2. Read the key information.
3. Find the next step.
4. Complete the form or contact action.
5. Confirm that the business receives the enquiry.
6. Check that the visitor receives a clear confirmation.

Test on more than one device and browser where practical.

## 8. Review security and maintenance

Mobile-first development does not remove the need for ordinary [website maintenance](/articles/tag/website-maintenance).

Confirm HTTPS, keep supported software updated, remove unused components and maintain backups. Forms should transmit information securely, and access to customer data should be restricted appropriately.

A website also needs an owner responsible for updating business details, service descriptions and contact information when circumstances change.

## A practical pre-launch checklist

- [ ] No unnecessary horizontal scrolling.
- [ ] Navigation works on small screens.
- [ ] Main text is readable without zooming.
- [ ] Images are optimised.
- [ ] Important buttons and links work.
- [ ] Forms have labels and useful error messages.
- [ ] Telephone and messaging links work.
- [ ] Accessibility has been reviewed.
- [ ] Performance has been measured.
- [ ] Security, backups and maintenance responsibilities are clear.


> **Already have a website?** Use the [website assessment](/#audit) to review possible improvement areas.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is mobile-first design the same as responsive design?

They are related but not identical. Mobile-first describes the development approach; responsive design describes how a layout adapts to different screen sizes. A mobile-first project will commonly use responsive techniques.

### Does a mobile-friendly website need an app?

No. Many businesses can provide a useful mobile experience through a well-built website. An app should be considered only when its additional capabilities justify the cost and maintenance.

### Should every page have a WhatsApp button?

Not necessarily. Use contact options that suit the business and its customers. Too many floating buttons can obstruct content and make mobile pages harder to use.

## Conclusion

A mobile-first website should help people understand a business and complete important tasks without friction. Start with layout, navigation, readable content, performance, accessibility and working contact journeys.

These fundamentals matter whether a business serves Maboloka, Soshanguve, Centurion or a wider market. Test the experience with real users and real devices, then improve it based on evidence.

When customers search for a nearby service, they usually want more than a list of websites. They want to know which businesses provide the service, whether those businesses can help in their area and how to contact them.

Local [SEO](/services/seo) helps a business communicate that information clearly.

For businesses serving [Maboloka](/locations/maboloka), [Soshanguve](/locations/soshanguve), [Centurion](/locations/centurion) and surrounding areas, the objective is not to mention every place name as often as possible. It is to build accurate business information, useful website content and credible signals that help customers find an appropriate provider.

## 1. Understand how local results work

Google's official [local ranking guidance](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091?hl=en) describes three broad factors: relevance, distance and prominence.

- **Relevance:** How well the business matches what the person is looking for.
- **Distance:** How far the business is from the searcher or the location in the query.
- **Prominence:** How well-known the business is, informed by signals such as links and reviews.

These factors are not a simple formula a business can control completely. Local results may vary by search location, query and competition.

## 2. Keep business information accurate

If the business is eligible for a [Google Business Profile](/articles/tag/google-business-profile), review the profile for accuracy.

Check its name, category, contact details, hours, website and relevant service information. Use genuine photographs and keep important information up to date.

Service-area businesses must follow Google's eligibility and address rules. Do not create fictional offices or represent a service area as a staffed business location when that is not true.

Google explicitly says that there is no way to request or pay for better local ranking. Treat guaranteed Maps positions with caution.

## 3. Make the website useful to local customers

Your website should explain what the business does, who it serves and how customers can take the next step.

A useful service page should describe:
- The service and the problem it addresses.
- Who the service is suitable for.
- What is included.
- Important conditions or limitations.
- How customers request information or a quotation.
- The areas genuinely served, where relevant.

A business serving Soshanguve might explain how customers in the area arrange an appointment. A business operating in Centurion could clarify its service coverage and how enquiries are handled. A provider working around Maboloka could answer practical questions about availability and access.

These details should reflect actual operations rather than being inserted solely to influence rankings.

## 4. Avoid thin location pages

Creating a separate page for every suburb is not automatically a good strategy.

If ten pages repeat the same paragraphs and change only the town name, they provide little additional value. Instead, create a distinct page when there is enough genuinely useful information to justify it.

Consider whether the page can explain local service arrangements, relevant examples, delivery or travel conditions, frequently asked questions or customer needs specific to that area.

Google's [people-first content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) encourages useful content created for people rather than pages produced primarily to manipulate search results.

> **Want to improve your website's visibility?** Check our [SEO Audit](/services/seo#audit) to explore its digital services.

## 5. Improve on-page foundations

Every important page should have a descriptive title, a clear main heading and content that matches its purpose.

Review:
- Page titles and meta descriptions.
- Heading hierarchy.
- Internal links between related pages.
- Image descriptions where appropriate.
- Canonical URLs and redirects.
- Indexing settings and XML sitemap.
- Mobile usability and performance.
- HTTPS and broken links.

Technical SEO helps search engines access and understand a website. It cannot compensate for an unclear service or inaccurate business information.

## 6. Earn trust through genuine reviews

Reviews can help potential customers understand other people's experiences. Ask real customers for honest feedback without buying reviews, creating fake accounts or pressuring people to leave positive comments.

Respond professionally. Thank customers for useful feedback, address concerns constructively and avoid revealing private information in public replies.

Businesses serving Maboloka, Soshanguve and Centurion should build a reputation through actual service delivery. Trust cannot be manufactured reliably through a collection of artificial testimonials.

## 7. Build relevant local references

Accurate mentions on relevant directories, professional associations, supplier websites and legitimate community resources can help people discover a business.

Prioritise quality and consistency over volume. Correct old telephone numbers and addresses where possible. Avoid paying for irrelevant links or submitting the business to low-quality directories simply to increase listing counts.

## 8. Measure enquiries, not just rankings

Use [Google Search](/articles/tag/google-search) Console to review search impressions, clicks and queries. If a Google Business Profile is available, review the performance information provided there.

Track business outcomes too:
- Relevant calls and enquiries.
- Quote requests.
- Bookings.
- Visits to key service pages.
- Qualified leads and sales.

Search positions can vary by place and device. A single manual search is not a complete measure of local visibility.

> **Not sure what needs attention first?** Visit our [Mogen Services](/services) to learn more about our offers.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can a business based in Maboloka appear for searches in Centurion?

It may be possible for relevant organic results, depending on the query and competition, but Google Maps results also consider distance. Businesses must represent their actual locations and service areas honestly.

### Is Google Business Profile enough for local SEO?

It can be an important part of the strategy, but it does not replace a useful website, accurate information, a good reputation and a clear customer experience.

### How long does local SEO take?

There is no universal timeline. Results depend on competition, the website's current state, the business's reputation and the work required. Avoid providers who guarantee specific rankings or dates.

## Conclusion

[Local SEO](/articles/tag/local-seo) works best when it reflects the real business. Accurate profiles, useful service pages, genuine reviews and sound technical foundations help customers understand whether a business can meet their needs.

For businesses serving Maboloka, Soshanguve, Centurion and nearby communities, focus on relevance and trust rather than repeating location names. Measure qualified enquiries and keep improving the parts of the customer journey that matter.

  [Email marketing](/articles/tag/email-marketing) can help a [small business](/articles/tag/small-business) keep customers informed, share useful advice, introduce relevant services and build relationships over time. It can also become a source of frustration when people receive messages they did not expect, cannot unsubscribe easily or discover that their details have been shared without their understanding.

  For South African businesses, permission-based marketing must be considered alongside the Protection of Personal Information Act, commonly known as [POPIA](/articles/tag/popia). Section 69 addresses direct marketing through unsolicited electronic communications, including email, SMS and other electronic channels covered by the legislation.

  The rules are important for more than large mailing lists. A small business sending occasional promotional emails must still think carefully about why it collected the recipient's information, what permission or other applicable basis it relies on, and how it handles objections.

  This guide explains how to build a more responsible email marketing process while keeping campaigns practical and useful.

  It is general information rather than legal advice. Businesses with complex customer databases, multiple marketing channels or uncertain consent records should obtain advice appropriate to their circumstances.

  ## 1. Understand the difference between an enquiry and marketing permission

  One of the most common mistakes is assuming that anyone who contacts a business has agreed to receive promotional messages indefinitely.

  A person may submit an enquiry because they want a quotation, request information about a service, or ask a specific question. That action does not automatically mean they want ongoing promotional emails about unrelated offers.

  Consider these examples:

  - A visitor requests a quotation for a website.
  - A customer purchases a service and provides an email address for transaction-related communication.
  - A visitor subscribes to a newsletter after being told what it contains.
  - A person receives a business card or sends a message through [social media](/articles/tag/social-media).

  These situations have different contexts and purposes. A business should not treat every email address it encounters as a marketing subscriber.

  The Information Regulator's [guidance notes on direct marketing](https://inforegulator.org.za/guidance-notes/) explain the application of POPIA to direct marketing, including electronic communication under section 69.

  Start by deciding what the communication is intended to do. A message necessary to respond to a specific customer request is different from a campaign promoting additional products or services.

  ## 2. Understand section 69 of POPIA

  Section 69 regulates the processing of personal information for direct marketing through unsolicited electronic communications.

  In broad terms, the section provides that this processing is prohibited unless the data subject has given consent or qualifies for the existing-customer exception set out in the Act.

  The existing-customer exception is not a blanket permission to send any promotion to anyone who has ever bought something.

  Section 69(3) sets conditions. Among other things, the contact details must have been obtained in the context of a sale of a product or service, the marketing must concern the responsible party's own similar products or services, and the customer must have been given a reasonable opportunity to object without charge or unnecessary formality.

  That opportunity must be provided when the details are collected and with each subsequent marketing communication where the customer has not initially refused the use.

  Read the [Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013](https://www.justice.gov.za/legislation/acts/2013-004.pdf) alongside the applicable regulations and the Information Regulator's guidance.

  ### What about a new subscriber?

  Where the business needs consent for unsolicited electronic direct marketing, section 69(2) provides that a person who has not previously withheld consent may be approached only once to request it.

  The consent request must follow the applicable prescribed requirements. A business should not treat a non-response as permission or repeatedly contact someone who has already refused.

  The detailed requirements are important, so do not build a campaign around a simplified assumption that one checkbox or a general privacy notice automatically makes every subsequent marketing message lawful.

  ## 3. Account for the amended regulations

  [South Africa](/articles/tag/south-africa)'s POPIA regulations were amended in April 2025, including the provisions governing requests for consent for unsolicited electronic direct marketing.

  The Information Regulator's [amended regulations](https://inforegulator.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/POPIA-2021-Regulations-FINAL-21-Jan-2025.pdf) replace Regulation 6 with requirements addressing written consent, Form 4 or a substantially similar approach, and methods through which a consent request can be made.

  The amended text refers to channels including email, telephone, SMS and WhatsApp, as well as other specified methods. It also addresses recording consent requests made telephonically and through automated calling machines.

  Importantly, Regulation 6.4 states that opting out does not constitute consent for unsolicited electronic direct marketing.

  This is a reason to review old signup processes rather than assuming that a mechanism designed several years ago still meets the current requirements.

  ### Review your consent mechanism

  Check whether your process:

  - Explains that the person is being asked to consent to direct marketing.
  - Identifies the responsible party.
  - Specifies the goods or services to be marketed as required.
  - Records the person's decision and the date.
  - Captures the preferred communication method where applicable.
  - Stores evidence that can be retrieved later.
  - Avoids treating silence or an opt-out as consent.

  The appropriate implementation depends on the circumstances and the current legal requirements. For a detailed review, consult the official regulation and obtain legal advice where necessary.

  ## 4. Build a clear subscription experience

  A newsletter signup should explain what the person is signing up to receive.

  Avoid vague promises such as "Stay connected" when the actual intention is to send frequent sales promotions.

  Instead, describe the expected content in straightforward language. For example, a business might explain that its newsletter contains practical business advice, occasional product updates and relevant service announcements.

  Be transparent about the organisation sending the messages. If multiple businesses or unrelated brands will receive subscriber information, do not conceal that fact behind a generic signup statement.

  Do not combine a necessary enquiry form with an ambiguous marketing opt-in that makes people think they must agree to advertising before they can request a quotation.

  Keep the choices understandable and the form usable on mobile devices.

  ### Store evidence of the decision

  A database entry containing only an email address is weak evidence of how that address became a marketing contact.

  Where consent is the applicable basis, maintain appropriate records of the consent request, the person's response, the date and the scope of permission.

  A simple record might include:

  - Subscriber identifier.
  - Contact address.
  - Source of the signup.
  - Date and method of the consent request.
  - Wording or version of the consent notice.
  - The response received.
  - The categories of marketing covered.
  - Any later withdrawal or objection.

  Keep only the information needed for the relevant purpose and protect the records against unauthorised access.

  ## 5. Do not purchase or casually reuse email lists

  Buying a mailing list may seem like a shortcut to reaching more customers, especially when a business is trying to grow quickly.

  But the fact that a third party possesses an email address does not establish that the business has permission to use it for its own direct marketing.

  A list may have been collected for another purpose, under a different relationship or with unclear permission. The business may not be able to establish what recipients were told or whether their preferences have changed.

  Before importing any existing list, ask:

  - How were the addresses collected?
  - What purpose was communicated to the people concerned?
  - Does the available evidence support the intended use?
  - Which organisation was identified in the original consent?
  - Have recipients objected or withdrawn consent?
  - Can the business demonstrate the applicable legal basis?

  If these questions cannot be answered, do not assume that the list is suitable for marketing.

  A smaller list of relevant people who genuinely want to hear from the business can be more useful than a large, poorly understood database.

  ## 6. Make unsubscribing straightforward

  Every marketing process needs a reliable way to record and respect objections.

  Section 69 requires direct marketing communications to identify the sender or the person on whose behalf the message is sent, and provide an address or other contact details through which the recipient can request that communications cease.

  Design the process so recipients can exercise this choice without unnecessary effort.

  Practical measures include:

  - A clear unsubscribe link where suitable.
  - A monitored contact method for opt-out requests.
  - A process for handling requests received by reply email.
  - A suppression list to prevent accidental re-importing.
  - Staff instructions for updating subscriber preferences.
  - A record of when the objection was received and processed.

  Do not require someone to log into an account, explain why they want to leave or navigate a long series of screens just to stop receiving marketing messages.

  The process should also work when a person contacts the business through a different channel. If someone asks a staff member to stop marketing messages, make sure that request reaches the people responsible for the mailing list.

  ### Keep a suppression record

  Deleting an unsubscribed person's address from one mailing list can create a problem if the same address is later imported from an old spreadsheet.

  A carefully controlled suppression mechanism helps prevent this.

  Keep only the minimum information needed to honour the objection and protect it appropriately. Do not use the suppression record as a reason to resume marketing.

  ## 7. Send content that is worth receiving

  Permission is a starting point, not a guarantee that every message will be useful.

  A successful campaign should provide a clear reason for the recipient to open it.

  Depending on the business, useful content might include:

  - Practical guidance related to the customer's needs.
  - Product or service updates that match the subscriber's stated interests.
  - Important information about a service the customer uses.
  - Relevant educational material.
  - Announcements that are genuinely useful to the intended audience.

  Avoid sending every announcement to every subscriber simply because the mailing platform allows it.

  A small business can start with a manageable schedule, such as a useful newsletter at a consistent interval, and adjust according to the needs of its audience.

  The correct frequency depends on the value of the content and what subscribers were told to expect. A business should not promise monthly updates and then start sending daily promotions without reviewing the scope of its communications.

  ## 8. Segment your list carefully

  Segmentation means dividing a subscriber list into relevant groups so messages better match the audience.

  A business might separate subscribers by the types of updates they selected or by an appropriate customer relationship.

  For example, a business selling several distinct services may allow people to choose which topics interest them. A subscriber interested in website maintenance may not want updates about unrelated products.

  Keep segmentation transparent and proportionate. Do not collect sensitive or unnecessary information just to create more elaborate marketing categories.

  Also remember that segmentation does not create legal permission by itself. A business still needs an appropriate basis for processing the personal information and sending the communication.

  Where possible, let subscribers manage their preferences and record changes accurately.

  ## 9. Protect the subscriber database

  An email list is a collection of personal information. It should be handled with appropriate security and access controls.

  Review the following:

  - Who can export the mailing list?
  - Are staff using shared accounts?
  - Is multi-factor authentication available?
  - Can former employees still access the database?
  - Are subscriber records included in backups?
  - Does the provider explain how information is stored and processed?
  - Are old records reviewed when they are no longer necessary?
  - Can the business retrieve records needed to demonstrate its decisions?

  If an external email marketing platform processes subscriber information on the business's behalf, review the service terms, security arrangements and responsibilities that apply.

  Do not upload the entire customer database to a new platform simply because it offers a convenient marketing feature. Establish what information is needed and whether the proposed use is appropriate.

  POPIA compliance involves more than a checkbox on a signup form. It also requires responsible handling of the personal information throughout the relevant processing activities.

  ## 10. Measure campaigns without losing sight of the customer

  Email [analytics](/articles/tag/analytics) can help a business understand whether its messages are useful.

  Depending on the platform, available measures may include delivery, opens, clicks, unsubscribes and conversions. Some measurements, particularly open rates, can be affected by privacy features and technical limitations, so they should not be treated as perfect evidence of human behaviour.

  Focus on questions that support decisions:

  - Are messages reaching the intended audience?
  - Are links working correctly?
  - Do subscribers engage with the information?
  - Which topics generate relevant visits or enquiries?
  - Are unsubscribe rates changing after a campaign?
  - Are the resulting enquiries appropriate for the business?

  Avoid interpreting a high open rate as proof that a campaign is profitable. The more important question is whether the communication supports the intended customer relationship and business objective.

  Keep tracking proportionate to the purpose and consider the privacy implications of the technologies used.

  **If your website collects email addresses, review the signup journey before expanding your campaigns.**

  > **Website assessment:** Use Mogen's [website assessment](/#assessment) to discuss the website forms and customer journey involved in collecting enquiries or newsletter subscriptions.

  ## A practical email marketing checklist

  Before sending a campaign, confirm that:

  - [ ] The purpose of the message is clear.
  - [ ] The intended recipients have an appropriate basis for receiving it.
  - [ ] Required consent evidence is available where consent is relied upon.
  - [ ] Existing-customer marketing meets the applicable conditions.
  - [ ] The sender is clearly identified.
  - [ ] Recipients can request that marketing stop through a suitable contact method.
  - [ ] Previous objections are respected.
  - [ ] The message matches the audience's expectations.
  - [ ] Subscriber information is protected.
  - [ ] The campaign links work on mobile devices.
  - [ ] Results and complaints are reviewed.
  - [ ] The process reflects current requirements rather than outdated assumptions.

  > **Current website offers:**
  > 
  > Review [Mogen's promotions page](/promotions) for published offers that may be relevant to your website and digital presence needs.

  ## Frequently asked questions

  ### Can I email a customer because they previously purchased from me?

  Sometimes, section 69(3) provides a limited existing-customer exception for marketing the responsible party's own similar products or services, subject to the conditions in the Act. A previous purchase is not blanket permission for every type of marketing.

  ### Can I ask someone to subscribe if they have not consented?

  Section 69(2) provides a limited once-only approach for requesting consent from a person who has not previously withheld it, where consent is required. The request must comply with the applicable requirements. Do not repeatedly ask after a refusal or treat silence as permission.

  ### Is an unsubscribe link enough to make an email campaign compliant?

  No. A suitable method for stopping messages is important, but it does not replace the need for an appropriate basis for sending the marketing in the first place or the other applicable requirements.

  ### Can I use a list of business email addresses found online?

  Do not assume that publicly available contact details automatically permit unsolicited electronic direct marketing. Establish the applicable legal basis and follow the relevant requirements before using the information for a campaign.

  ## Conclusion

  Responsible email marketing starts with a clear purpose, an appropriately obtained subscriber relationship and a reliable way to honour preferences.

  For South African businesses, section 69 of POPIA and the amended regulations provide important rules for unsolicited electronic direct marketing. A practical process should account for those requirements, maintain suitable evidence, protect subscriber information and make objections easy to exercise.

  Start by reviewing how your current list was collected, how permission is recorded and how unsubscribe requests are handled. Then improve the quality and relevance of the messages you send.

  A smaller, well-managed list can provide a stronger foundation for long-term customer relationships than a large database whose origins and permissions are unclear.
