  A [small business](/articles/tag/small-business) does not need to operate a large IT department to handle personal information. It may collect customer names, telephone numbers, email addresses, enquiry details, employee records or supplier contact information as part of ordinary operations.

  That information creates responsibilities.

  A security compromise can happen through a cyberattack, a lost device, an email sent to the wrong recipient, inappropriate access or a failure to protect records properly. The consequences may extend beyond technology: customers can be affected, operations may be disrupted and the business may need to take formal notification and recovery steps.

  The time to decide who does what is before an incident occurs.

  A written response plan helps staff recognise a possible compromise, escalate it to the right person, preserve relevant information and follow an organised process.

  For South African businesses, the Protection of Personal Information Act ([POPIA](/articles/tag/popia)) and the Information Regulator's guidance are important starting points. This article explains how to document a practical response process without treating a template as a substitute for legal or specialist security advice.

  ## 1. Understand what a security compromise can involve

  The Information Regulator describes a security compromise as an event affecting the security, confidentiality, integrity or availability of personal information, including accidental or unlawful loss, destruction, alteration, disclosure, processing or access.

  Examples include:

  - Sending personal information to the wrong email recipient.
  - Losing paperwork or a device containing inadequately protected information.
  - A cyberattack that exposes or alters personal information.
  - Unauthorised access by an employee or another person.
  - Sharing passwords or leaving personal information accessible to unauthorised people.

  A compromise does not have to begin with an advanced cyberattack. Ordinary operational mistakes can also expose information.

  The Information Regulator's [Fact Sheet: Handling of Security Compromises](https://inforegulator.org.za/2025/08/19/fact-sheet-handling-of-security-compromises/) explains examples of compromises and the notification process.

  Your procedure should therefore cover both digital and physical records. A business that stores customer details in email, paper forms and spreadsheets needs a process that applies to all those environments.

  ## 2. Assign responsibility before an incident occurs

  A response plan should make it clear who receives the first report and who has authority to coordinate the response.

  Under the Information Regulator's guidance, the Information Officer or Deputy Information Officer should report a security compromise to the Regulator and affected data subjects on behalf of the responsible party.

  The exact roles and internal reporting lines will depend on the organisation. Document them clearly instead of assuming that every employee knows whom to contact.

  A useful responsibility table might look like this:

  | Role | Responsibility to document |
  |---|---|
  | Employee or person discovering the issue | Report the suspected compromise promptly and preserve relevant information |
  | Incident coordinator | Maintain the incident record and coordinate internal actions |
  | Information Officer or Deputy Information Officer | Coordinate the required assessment and notification process |
  | IT or security support | Help contain the incident, investigate affected systems and restore services |
  | Management | Approve appropriate resources and operational decisions |
  | External service provider or operator | Notify the responsible party promptly when a compromise affects information processed on its behalf |

  In a small business, one person may perform several internal functions. The important point is that responsibilities are assigned and understood.

  The response plan should include current contact details and an alternative contact if the primary person is unavailable.

  ## 3. Document the first-response procedure

  Staff need simple instructions they can follow under pressure.

  A first-response checklist should explain what to do when someone suspects that personal information has been compromised.

  ### Step 1: Report the incident immediately

  Provide a clear reporting route, such as a designated business email address or direct contact with the incident coordinator.

  Staff should not be expected to determine the full legal classification of an event before reporting it internally.

  The procedure should encourage prompt escalation, even if the available information is incomplete.

  ### Step 2: Protect people and limit further exposure

  Depending on the incident, practical steps may include disabling a compromised account, revoking exposed credentials, restricting access to affected records or isolating an affected system with appropriate technical assistance.

  The response should avoid destroying information needed to understand the incident.

  Do not instruct untrained staff to take risky technical actions that could worsen the situation. The plan should explain when to involve qualified IT or security support.

  ### Step 3: Preserve relevant evidence

  Record what was observed and when. Preserve relevant messages, system alerts, access logs and other available records in a controlled manner.

  Avoid circulating copies of exposed personal information unnecessarily. The investigation should use the minimum information needed by authorised people.

  ### Step 4: Notify the designated responsible people

  Escalate the issue to the incident coordinator and Information Officer or Deputy Information Officer according to the documented process.

  If a third-party operator discovers a compromise involving information controlled by the business, the operator must notify the responsible party. The contract and incident procedure should make this communication route clear.

  ## 4. Record the facts without delaying urgent action

  The business needs a reliable record of what happened, what is known and what remains uncertain.

  Create an incident register with fields such as:

  | Field | Information to record |
  |---|---|
  | Incident reference | A unique internal identifier |
  | Date and time discovered | When the issue was first identified |
  | Reporter | The person or system that raised the alert |
  | Incident summary | A factual description of the suspected compromise |
  | Information involved | Categories of personal information potentially affected |
  | Systems or records | Relevant applications, devices, files or physical records |
  | People potentially affected | The known or estimated scope, where established |
  | Immediate actions | Steps taken to limit further exposure |
  | Responsible contacts | People notified internally and externally |
  | Notification record | Dates, methods and references for required notifications |
  | Outstanding questions | Facts that still need investigation |
  | Remediation | Corrective actions and their status |
  | Closure review | Findings, approvals and lessons learned |

  Restrict access to this register because it may contain sensitive incident details.

  Record facts separately from assumptions. For example, note that an account was accessed at a particular time if that is supported by logs, but do not describe information as stolen unless the evidence supports that conclusion.

  This discipline helps the business investigate the incident without presenting unverified conclusions as established facts.

  ## 5. Know the notification principle

  POPIA section 22 addresses notification of security compromises.

  The Information Regulator's published guidance states that security compromises must be reported regardless of their perceived risk level. It also explains that the responsible party should notify the Regulator and affected data subjects as soon as it is reasonably sure that a compromise has occurred.

  This has an important operational consequence: the business should not automatically wait for a complete forensic investigation before escalating the notification process.

  The information available at the beginning may be incomplete. The Regulator's guidance advises reporting as soon as reasonably practicable using the information available and updating the notification as further information becomes available.

  The response plan should therefore define a prompt decision and escalation process rather than requiring staff to finish every investigative task first.

  Read the [Information Regulator's security compromise fact sheet](https://inforegulator.org.za/2025/08/19/fact-sheet-handling-of-security-compromises/) and the official [Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013](https://www.gov.za/documents/protection-personal-information-act) when preparing your procedure.

  This article is general operational guidance, not legal advice. Businesses should confirm how the law and current regulatory guidance apply to their circumstances.

  ## 6. Document the notification workflow

  The response plan should identify who coordinates the notification process and where the required submissions are made.

  According to the Information Regulator, security compromise notifications under section 22 have been submitted through its eServices portal since 1 April 2025.

  The official [Information Regulator eServices portal](https://eservices.inforegulator.org.za/) provides a service for reporting security compromises.

  Document the following in your internal procedure:

  - Who prepares and coordinates the notification.
  - Who is authorised to submit it.
  - Which official portal or current reporting channel must be used.
  - What facts and supporting information should be collected.
  - How submission references and copies are retained.
  - Who coordinates communication with affected data subjects.
  - How additional information will be recorded and supplied when needed.

  Do not store portal passwords in the procedure itself. Record the responsible role and the approved secure method for obtaining access.

  The notification process should be reviewed against the Regulator's current instructions. Avoid relying indefinitely on an old form, saved screenshot or procedure that has not been checked for changes.

  ## 7. Prepare for communication with affected people

  A notification process should address both the Regulator and affected data subjects, as applicable under the relevant requirements.

  The Information Regulator's guidance explains that communication to data subjects should describe what happened and when, what steps are being taken to mitigate the impact, what advice may help the affected people and other relevant information that is known.

  Your internal plan should identify who prepares the communication and how it is checked before it is sent.

  The exact wording depends on the incident. A lost device, an incorrectly addressed email and an intrusion into a business application may involve different facts and different practical advice.

  Prepare a communication checklist rather than a single message that assumes every incident is the same.

  It should prompt the responsible people to verify:

  - What is known about the event.
  - Which categories of information may be affected.
  - Which people may need to be notified.
  - What the business has done to limit further exposure.
  - What practical guidance affected people may need.
  - Which contact route can be used for questions.
  - Whether further communication may be required.

  Avoid disclosing additional personal information while explaining the incident. Have the appropriate responsible person review the proposed communication and seek specialist advice when necessary.

  ## 8. Include suppliers and external operators

  Many small businesses depend on external providers for email, hosting, customer management, payroll, cloud storage and other services.

  A business should know which providers process personal information on its behalf and how to reach them during an incident.

  Maintain a supplier register with:

  - Provider and service name.
  - Type of information handled.
  - Business contact and emergency escalation route.
  - Relevant contract or processing agreement.
  - Provider notification requirements.
  - Responsibilities for investigation and remediation.
  - Available logs, reports or other evidence.
  - Procedure for ending access when the relationship ends.

  POPIA places responsibilities on responsible parties and also addresses the obligations of operators. The Information Regulator's guidance states that an operator must notify the responsible party when a compromise affects personal information it processes on that party's behalf.

  Make sure the relevant agreements and operating procedures support this communication.

  A contract alone is not a response plan. Staff still need to know whom to contact, what information to request and how to escalate an incident outside normal business hours where necessary.

  ## 9. Plan containment, recovery and prevention

  Notification is only one part of the response.

  The business also needs to address the cause of the incident, reduce further exposure and restore affected operations safely.

  Depending on the circumstances, actions may include:

  - Resetting compromised credentials.
  - Reviewing access permissions.
  - Applying security updates.
  - Restoring systems from verified backups.
  - Recovering lost or altered records.
  - Correcting a mistaken disclosure where possible.
  - Reviewing the security of supplier integrations.
  - Training staff on a process that failed.
  - Revising technical or organisational safeguards.

  Record who is responsible for each corrective action and when it is due.

  Do not close the incident merely because the website or application is working again. The business should also review whether the exposure has been contained, required notifications have been handled and further corrective work remains.

  After the incident, conduct a review focused on learning rather than assigning blame without evidence.

  Ask what allowed the incident to happen, whether the response process worked and which changes would reduce the likelihood or impact of a similar event.

  ## 10. Test the procedure before it is needed

  A document can appear complete while leaving staff unsure what to do in practice.

  Run a simple tabletop exercise using a hypothetical incident. For example, imagine that an employee sends a spreadsheet containing customer contact information to the wrong recipient.

  Ask the team:

  1. Who receives the first report?
  2. What information must be recorded immediately?
  3. Who decides which response actions are appropriate?
  4. Who must be notified internally?
  5. How will the Information Officer be contacted?
  6. Where will the incident and notification records be stored?
  7. How will the business verify that corrective actions are completed?

  The exercise should test the process, not expose real customer data.

  Record any gaps and update the procedure. Review it when staff responsibilities, suppliers, systems or relevant regulatory guidance change.

  ## 11. A practical document pack for a small business

  A small business does not necessarily need a lengthy manual. A concise, well-maintained pack may be more useful than a complex document that nobody follows.

  Consider maintaining the following:

  | Document | Purpose |
  |---|---|
  | Security compromise response procedure | Defines the sequence of actions |
  | Roles and contact register | Identifies the people responsible for the response |
  | Incident register template | Records the facts and decisions |
  | Personal information inventory | Helps identify what information is held and where |
  | Supplier and operator register | Identifies external services and escalation routes |
  | Notification checklist | Helps coordinate required communications |
  | Recovery checklist | Records containment and restoration tasks |
  | Post-incident review template | Captures lessons and corrective actions |
  | Staff reporting instructions | Explains how employees raise a concern |

  These documents should be proportionate to the business. A small professional practice may have a simpler system than a business processing large volumes of sensitive information, but both need a clear process appropriate to their risks and obligations.

  Store the documents securely, control who can edit them and maintain version information so staff can identify the current procedure.

  ## Frequently asked questions

  ### Does every small business need a written incident response plan?

  The appropriate documentation depends on the business's operations, information and obligations. A written procedure is a practical way to establish responsibilities and make the response repeatable. Businesses should confirm the specific requirements that apply to them.

  ### Should a business wait until a security compromise is fully investigated before reporting it?

  The Information Regulator's published guidance says the responsible party should notify the Regulator and affected data subjects as soon as it is reasonably sure a compromise has occurred. It also advises reporting with the information available and updating the notification as more facts emerge. Confirm the current requirements for your situation.

  ### What if the incident occurs at a service provider?

  The business should have an agreed route for the provider to notify the responsible party promptly. The responsible party should then follow its documented assessment and notification process in accordance with the applicable requirements.

  ### Is a lost laptop automatically a reportable security compromise?

  A lost device may involve a security compromise if personal information is affected. The facts matter, including what information was stored, how it was protected and what is known about access. The Information Regulator's guidance states that security compromises must be reported irrespective of their perceived risk level. Seek appropriate advice when assessing a specific incident.

  ### Can a business use a template from the internet?

  A template can be a starting point, but it should be adapted to the business's actual systems, roles, suppliers and procedures. Check that it reflects current official guidance and does not promise compliance simply because a form has been completed.

  ## Conclusion

  A security compromise can create confusion at precisely the time a business needs to act clearly and promptly.

  A documented response plan helps staff report incidents, preserve relevant information, contact the right people and coordinate containment, notification and recovery. It also makes it easier to learn from an incident and improve the safeguards that protect personal information.

  Start by documenting responsibilities, a practical first-response checklist and a reliable incident register. Add supplier contacts, notification steps and recovery procedures that reflect the way your business actually operates.

  Review the plan periodically and check it against current Information Regulator guidance. The objective is not simply to possess a policy, but to make sure authorised people can follow it when it matters.

[Email marketing](/articles/tag/email-marketing) can help a [small business](/articles/tag/small-business) stay in contact with customers, share useful information and introduce relevant products or services. It can also become an expensive and frustrating exercise when messages are sent to people who never asked to receive them.

A common mistake is assuming that having someone's email address gives a business permission to send promotional messages.

In [South Africa](/articles/tag/south-africa), the Protection of Personal Information Act ([POPIA](/articles/tag/popia)) regulates the processing of personal information for [direct marketing](/articles/tag/direct-marketing) through unsolicited electronic communications. Section 69 sets out the conditions under which this type of marketing may take place.

The Information Regulator has also published guidance on direct marketing and the regulations have been amended since their original publication. Businesses should therefore be careful about relying on old email marketing advice or outdated interpretations of the rules.

This article explains how a small business can build and manage a permission-based email list while keeping its marketing process practical.

It is general business information, not legal advice. Businesses with complex marketing arrangements, existing databases or uncertain consent records should obtain appropriate professional advice.

## Why permission matters

An email address is personal information when it relates to an identifiable person. POPIA defines direct marketing broadly, including approaches made to promote or offer goods and services.

Section 69 deals specifically with direct marketing through unsolicited electronic communications. It includes examples such as email, SMS, fax and automatic calling machines.

The Act's definition of electronic communication is also broad. It covers text, voice, sound or image messages sent over an electronic communications network and stored until collected by the recipient.

This matters when a business uses more than one marketing channel. Email is not the only electronic communication that needs consideration.

A business collecting contact details from customers in [Maboloka](/locations/maboloka), [Soshanguve](/locations/soshanguve), [Centurion](/locations/centurion) or elsewhere should have a clear reason for collecting those details and a suitable basis for using them.

The relevant legal starting points are [section 69 of POPIA](https://www.justice.gov.za/legislation/acts/2013-004.pdf) and the Information Regulator's [guidance notes on direct marketing](https://inforegulator.org.za/guidance-notes/).

## 1. Understand the two routes under section 69

Section 69(1) generally prohibits processing personal information for direct marketing through unsolicited electronic communication unless the data subject has given consent or qualifies for the existing-customer exception in section 69(3).

These are two different routes. A business should not assume that every person who has ever interacted with it qualifies for the customer exception.

### Route A: The person has consented

A business can market electronically where the person has provided the required consent.

Consent should be voluntary, specific and informed. The business should be able to explain what the person agreed to receive and maintain evidence of that agreement.

### Route B: The person is an existing customer

Section 69(3) provides a limited exception for marketing to an existing customer.

The exception applies only when the relevant conditions are met:

- The business obtained the person's contact details in the context of a sale of a product or service.
- The marketing relates to the business's own similar products or services.
- The person received a reasonable opportunity to object, free of charge and without unnecessary formality, when the information was collected.
- The person is given that opportunity again in each marketing communication if they have not initially refused.

These conditions are important.

A person who merely requested a quotation is not automatically covered by the existing-customer exception. Neither is someone whose details were collected from a public directory, a networking event or a purchased database.

If the business cannot confidently establish that the exception applies, it should not assume that the address can be used for promotional email marketing.

## 2. Understand the one-time consent request

Section 69(2) allows a responsible party to approach a person whose consent is required, provided that the person has not previously withheld consent, only once to request that consent.

The request must follow the prescribed requirements.

This is not permission to send an unsolicited promotional email and then treat the recipient's silence as agreement.

A consent request should be a genuine request for permission, not a disguised sales campaign.

It should identify the business, explain the products or services to be marketed and give the person a clear choice.

The amended POPIA Regulations provide more detail about the form and methods that may be used for requesting consent. Regulation 6 allows a form substantially similar to Form 4 or another expedient, free and reasonably accessible method, including email, telephone, SMS and WhatsApp. Requests made telephonically must be electronically recorded in the circumstances specified by the regulations.

The amendment was published for implementation with immediate effect on 17 April 2025. The official [Government Notice 6126](https://www.justice.gov.za/legislation/notices/2025/20250417-gg52523gon6126-POPIA-Regulations-Amendment.pdf) and the [amended POPIA Regulations](https://inforegulator.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/POPIA-2021-Regulations-FINAL-21-Jan-2025.pdf) provide the relevant detail.

## 3. Design a clear newsletter sign-up form

A website sign-up form is often the simplest way to build a permission-based list.

However, the form should explain what the visitor is agreeing to receive.

Avoid a vague checkbox that simply says "I agree" without identifying the marketing purpose.

A more useful form should explain:

- The identity of the business.
- The type of marketing messages the person will receive.
- The products or services that may be promoted.
- The intended communication channel.
- Where the person can find further privacy information.
- How the person can withdraw consent or ask for marketing to stop.

The form should make the choice clear and should not rely on preselected options that make the person's intention uncertain.

### Example of clearer sign-up wording

A business might use wording along these lines, adapted to its actual marketing activities and reviewed against the applicable requirements:

"I agree to receive occasional email updates from [Business Name] about its [specified products or services]. I understand that I can ask to stop receiving these marketing emails."

The business must identify itself and specify what it intends to market. It should not use broad wording to obtain permission for unrelated future campaigns.

The official regulations include Form 4, which identifies the responsible party, the goods or services to be marketed and the data subject's consent. A business should use the current requirements when designing its own process rather than copying an old template without review.

The Information Regulator maintains a [POPIA forms page](https://inforegulator.org.za/popia-forms/) where Form 4 is listed.

## 4. Do not confuse an enquiry with marketing permission

A customer may submit a contact form because they want a quotation, ask a question or request a callback.

That action should not automatically add the person's email address to a recurring newsletter list.

The purpose of collecting information matters.

For example:

| Customer action | What it normally tells the business |
| --- | --- |
| Requests a quotation | Wants information about a particular service |
| Submits a contact form | Wants the business to respond to an enquiry |
| Registers for a newsletter | Wants the specified marketing updates |
| Completes a purchase | Becomes a customer, subject to the applicable conditions |
| Downloads a document | Wants the requested resource; this does not automatically establish newsletter consent |

A business can provide a useful enquiry process without bundling unrelated marketing permission into it.

If the person wants to subscribe, make that a clear and separate choice.

This also makes it easier for the business to understand which contacts belong in its marketing database and which should only be retained for the purpose of responding to an enquiry.

## 5. Keep evidence of consent

A business should be able to demonstrate why a contact is on its marketing list.

A spreadsheet or marketing platform can help, provided that the business records enough information to understand the permission it obtained.

Useful fields may include:

| Record | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Contact identifier | Identifies the person or record |
| Date and time | Helps establish when permission was obtained |
| Collection method | Records whether consent came from a website, email or another channel |
| Consent wording or version | Shows what the person was told |
| Marketing purpose | Identifies the products or services covered |
| Preferred channel | Records the channel selected by the person |
| Evidence reference | Points to the relevant form submission or record |
| Withdrawal date | Records when consent was withdrawn or marketing was stopped |

Do not collect more information than the business needs.

If the newsletter only requires an email address, asking for an identity number, physical address and other unrelated details creates unnecessary data management responsibilities.

The purpose of keeping consent records is not to build a larger personal information database. It is to maintain enough evidence to manage the marketing process responsibly.

## 6. Make unsubscribing straightforward

People should be able to stop receiving marketing messages without unnecessary difficulty.

Section 69(4) requires every direct marketing communication to contain the identity of the sender or the person on whose behalf the message is sent, together with an address or other contact details to which the recipient can send a request that the communication cease.

In practical terms, the business should make its identity clear and provide a working way for the recipient to ask for marketing to stop.

A visible unsubscribe link is a useful way to achieve this in email campaigns.

Avoid processes that require a customer to telephone during business hours, explain why they want to leave the list or complete an unnecessarily complicated form.

When someone withdraws permission or objects, update the marketing records promptly.

A suppression list can help prevent a person who has unsubscribed from being accidentally re-imported during a future database upload. The suppression process should be designed carefully so that the business does not continue using the address for marketing simply because an old spreadsheet still contains it.

## 7. Treat the existing-customer exception carefully

The existing-customer exception can be useful, but it is not a general permission to market to every past contact.

Consider a business that sells a particular service and obtains the customer's email address during that sale.

The business may be able to market its own similar products or services under section 69(3), provided that all the conditions are met.

It should not assume that this allows it to:

- Market unrelated services.
- Share the customer's address with unrelated businesses for their marketing.
- Add the person to a broad newsletter without considering the applicable conditions.
- Ignore an objection.
- Continue marketing after the person has asked for it to stop.

Keep the exception narrow and document why the business believes the conditions apply.

If a customer has purchased one service, a relevant offer about a similar service may be different from an unrelated third-party promotion.

When the distinction is unclear, obtain appropriate legal advice rather than stretching the exception to cover the entire database.

## 8. Avoid purchased and scraped email lists

Buying a list of email addresses can look like a shortcut to reaching more potential customers.

It can also introduce significant compliance and marketing problems.

The business may not know:

- How the addresses were collected.
- Whether the individuals were informed about the intended use.
- Whether consent was obtained for the business's marketing purpose.
- Whether the contact details are accurate.
- Whether people have already objected.
- Whether the list contains outdated or duplicated records.

A public email address is not automatically permission to send promotional email.

Likewise, a person handing over a business card at an event has not necessarily agreed to receive a recurring marketing newsletter.

A smaller list built through clear, relevant sign-up choices is generally more useful than a large database with uncertain permission.

## 9. Make the newsletter worth receiving

Permission is only the starting point. A business still needs to give subscribers a reason to remain on the list.

A newsletter should have a clear purpose.

Depending on the business, it might include:

- Practical advice related to the products or services.
- Announcements about relevant developments.
- Useful maintenance or planning reminders.
- New resources or guides.
- Relevant product or service information.
- Genuine business updates.

Avoid sending messages simply because the marketing calendar says it is time to send something.

Before each campaign, ask:

- Is this information relevant to the people receiving it?
- Does it fit the purpose they agreed to?
- Is the subject line accurate?
- Can the recipient identify the sender?
- Is there a straightforward way to stop future marketing?
- Have the links and contact details been checked?

Consistency is useful, but frequency should be appropriate to the audience and the type of content being sent.

## 10. Protect the marketing database

A marketing list is a business asset, but it is also a collection of personal information that needs appropriate protection.

Limit access to staff who need it. Use suitable account security and avoid sharing full customer lists through informal channels.

Consider:

- Strong passwords and multi-factor authentication.
- Access permissions based on job responsibilities.
- Secure storage of exported contact lists.
- Review of marketing platform providers.
- Appropriate handling of backups.
- Removal of unnecessary duplicate records.
- A documented process for access and deletion requests.
- A procedure for handling security incidents.

If an external email marketing platform processes personal information on behalf of the business, review the relationship and the applicable POPIA responsibilities. The Act contains requirements relating to operators and security safeguards.

Do not assume that moving a contact list into a cloud platform transfers all responsibility to the provider.

## 11. Measure useful outcomes, not just list size

A large subscriber count does not necessarily indicate an effective marketing programme.

A small business should focus on whether its messages are reaching the intended audience and contributing to useful business outcomes.

Relevant indicators may include:

| Metric | What it can help explain |
| --- | --- |
| New permitted subscribers | Whether the sign-up process is attracting interest |
| Unsubscribes | Whether the content or frequency needs review |
| Bounces | Whether contact information is valid |
| Clicks | Whether readers are engaging with links |
| Website visits | Whether campaigns are encouraging further exploration |
| Enquiries | Whether marketing is generating relevant business conversations |
| Sales | Whether campaigns contribute to commercial outcomes |

Do not interpret an open rate as a perfect measure of whether a person read a message. Email privacy features and automated image loading can affect open tracking.

Compare campaigns over time and use several indicators rather than relying on one metric.

Also avoid collecting extra personal information solely to improve marketing reports. The business should have a clear purpose for every additional data field it stores.

## 12. A practical implementation checklist

A small business can begin improving its email marketing process without adopting a complex marketing automation platform.

**Step 1: Review the current list.**

Identify where the addresses came from and whether the business has evidence of the relevant consent or can establish that the existing-customer exception applies.

**Step 2: Separate enquiries from subscribers.**

Do not automatically add every contact form submission to the newsletter database.

**Step 3: Review the sign-up wording.**

Make the business identity, marketing purpose and communication channel clear.

**Step 4: Update the consent process.**

Review section 69 and the current regulations, including the applicable Form 4 requirements and permitted consent-request methods.

**Step 5: Keep evidence.**

Store the consent record and the information needed to understand what the person agreed to receive.

**Step 6: Check every campaign template.**

Confirm the sender's identity and provide a straightforward way to request that marketing stops.

**Step 7: Test the unsubscribe process.**

Verify that a request is received, recorded and acted upon.

**Step 8: Review access and storage.**

Ensure that only authorised people and appropriate service providers can access the marketing database.

**Step 9: Monitor campaign performance.**

Focus on relevant engagement and business outcomes rather than subscriber numbers alone.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I send marketing emails to everyone who has contacted my business?

No. An enquiry does not automatically establish permission for recurring marketing. Section 69 provides a consent route and a limited existing-customer exception, each with specific conditions.

### Does an unsubscribe link count as consent?

No. The amended POPIA Regulations expressly state that an opt-out does not constitute consent for the purposes of section 69(2).

### Can I use WhatsApp to request marketing consent?

The amended regulations identify WhatsApp among the methods that may be used for requesting consent, subject to the applicable requirements. The business should ensure that the request is genuine, appropriately recorded and compliant with the relevant provisions.

### Can an existing customer receive marketing without giving fresh consent?

Section 69(3) provides a limited exception for a customer's own similar products or services, provided all the conditions are met. It is not a general permission to market unrelated products or share customer details.

### Do I need a large email marketing platform?

Not necessarily. A small business can start with a manageable system that stores permission records, sends appropriate messages and processes unsubscribe requests reliably. The system should be selected according to the business's actual requirements.

## Conclusion

Email marketing works best when people understand why they are receiving messages and have made a meaningful choice to receive them.

For South African small businesses, that means understanding POPIA section 69, distinguishing enquiries from marketing subscriptions, applying the existing-customer exception carefully and keeping evidence of permission.

A well-managed list does not need to be enormous. It needs to be relevant, responsibly maintained and supported by content that subscribers actually find useful.

Build the permission process properly, make it easy to stop receiving messages and treat customer information with care. These practices support more sustainable marketing and help protect the trust on which long-term customer relationships depend.

Growing a [small business](/articles/tag/small-business) involves more than finding customers. Business owners must explain their services, build trust, manage enquiries and decide where limited time and money will have the greatest effect.

Digital tools can help with these tasks, but having a website, [social media](/articles/tag/social-media) account or advertising campaign is not automatically a business strategy. The value comes from choosing the right tools, connecting them to clear objectives and maintaining them as the business changes.

For businesses in [Gauteng](/articles/tag/gauteng) and elsewhere in [South Africa](/articles/tag/south-africa), a practical digital approach starts with the customer: what do people need to know, where do they look for solutions, and what would make them confident enough to contact you?

Mogen works across [web development](/services/web-development), [SEO](/services/seo) and [digital marketing](/services/digital-marketing). This article explains how these areas can complement one another and how a small business can prioritise them without trying to do everything at once.

## Start with your business objective

Before choosing a digital service, identify the problem you want to solve.

Common objectives include:

- Helping potential customers understand your services.
- Improving the quality of enquiries.
- Making important business information easier to find.
- Reaching customers in a defined service area.
- Explaining a new offer or product.
- Reducing repetitive questions by publishing useful information.
- Building a more consistent and credible online presence.

Make the objective specific enough to evaluate. “Improve our online presence” is a starting point, but “help prospective customers understand our three main services and request a quotation” is easier to turn into a practical plan.

Also establish a baseline. Record how enquiries currently arrive, which services generate revenue and what customers frequently ask before buying. You can then decide whether your biggest problem is website clarity, discoverability, marketing reach or the process used to handle leads.

## 1. Web development: give customers a useful place to start

Your website can act as a central source of information about your business. Unlike a profile on a third-party platform, a website gives you more control over how your services are organised and presented.

A useful small-business website should answer several questions quickly:

- What does the business offer?
- Who is the service intended for?
- What makes the offer relevant to the customer?
- Where does the business operate?
- How can someone make an enquiry?
- What should the customer expect next?

The right level of complexity depends on the business. A service provider with one main offering may need a focused website with clear service and contact information. A company with several distinct services may benefit from separate pages that explain each offering in more detail.

Prioritise clarity, mobile usability, readable content and working contact methods before investing in elaborate visual effects.

It is also important to plan for ongoing responsibility. Websites require decisions about domain registration, hosting, maintenance, updates and future changes. Decide who will handle those tasks and what support is available after launch.

## 2. SEO: help relevant customers discover your business

Search engine optimisation helps search engines understand your website and helps people decide whether a search result is relevant to them.

For a business that serves a defined area, local SEO may be an appropriate starting point. This can involve maintaining accurate business information, improving service pages, answering customer questions and ensuring that online listings reflect the real business.

For example, a business serving [Soshanguve](/locations/soshanguve) and [Centurion](/locations/centurion) should describe its actual service coverage rather than trying to appear everywhere. A business in [Maboloka](/locations/maboloka) should provide useful information to customers in its genuine market, without creating misleading location claims.

SEO is not a substitute for a good service or a clear website. It is also not an instant route to the top of Google. Search performance depends on multiple factors, including relevance, competition and the quality of the information available to users.

Google's [SEO Starter Guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/seo-starter-guide) is a useful reference for understanding the foundations. Its guidance on [helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) also reinforces the importance of creating material for people rather than publishing pages solely to attract search traffic.

> **Assess your website:** Use the [Mogen SEO Audit](https://www.mogen.co.za/services/seo#audit) to identify possible areas for improvement before deciding on your next step.

## 3. Digital marketing: reach the right audience

A useful website and a discoverable search presence do not eliminate every need for active marketing. Some businesses need to introduce a new service, promote a time-sensitive offer or reach an audience that may not yet be searching for what they provide.

Digital marketing can include content distribution, email communication, paid advertising and social media activity. The appropriate mix depends on the audience, budget, offer and capacity to handle responses.

Before launching a campaign, answer five questions:

1. **Audience:** Who is most likely to need this offer?
2. **Message:** What problem does it solve, and why should someone care?
3. **Destination:** Where should interested people go to learn more?
4. **Action:** What should they do next?
5. **Measurement:** How will you judge whether the campaign was worthwhile?

Avoid spreading a small budget across many platforms without a clear reason. Start with a focused experiment, establish what success means and evaluate the results before expanding.

If the campaign produces enquiries, consider whether they are relevant and whether your business can respond promptly. A large number of clicks is not necessarily evidence of commercial success.

## 4. Connect your website, SEO and marketing

These services are most useful when they support a coherent customer journey.

Consider a small professional service business in Gauteng.

A potential customer discovers a useful article through a search engine or a marketing post. The customer visits the website, reads a service page, checks the business details and submits an enquiry. The business then responds with the information needed to move the conversation forward.

Each part has a role:

| Digital activity | Main role | Example of a useful measure |
|---|---|---|
| Website development | Explain the offer and provide a clear next step | Enquiries completed successfully |
| SEO | Help relevant people discover useful pages | Relevant organic clicks and enquiries |
| Content marketing | Answer questions and communicate expertise | Meaningful engagement and assisted enquiries |
| Paid campaigns | Test or expand reach for a defined offer | Cost per qualified enquiry |
| Follow-up process | Turn interest into a business conversation | Response time and enquiry-to-sale rate |

The measures should match the objective. A new website may initially be judged on usability and whether customers can complete key actions. A search campaign may need more time before meaningful trends emerge. An advertising campaign should be evaluated against its actual costs and the value of the business it generates.

Do not assume that every result comes from one channel. Customers may encounter a business through several touchpoints before making contact.

## 5. Choose priorities that match your stage of growth

A business does not need to purchase every service at once.

### If you are starting out

Concentrate on the essentials: a clear description of your offer, reliable contact details, a suitable online home and an understanding of your customers.

Make sure the website communicates what you do and how to enquire. Establish the correct business information on relevant platforms, and collect genuine customer feedback as your business develops.

### If you have a website but few enquiries

Review the existing customer journey before assuming you need a complete rebuild or a large advertising budget.

Ask whether visitors can understand the offer, whether the contact process works on mobile, whether the service pages answer common questions and whether the website attracts the right audience.

Use available analytics and direct customer feedback to identify the main problem. Improve the weakest part first.

### If customers know your business but cannot find it online

Check your search presence, business information and website structure. Improve important service pages and publish content that answers questions your actual customers ask.

For eligible local businesses, Google's guidance on [improving local rankings](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091?hl=en-en) explains the importance of relevance, distance and prominence.

### If you are ready to expand

Once the foundations are working, test targeted marketing campaigns, develop more detailed content or expand the website to support additional services.

Set a budget you can sustain, measure meaningful results and retain enough operational capacity to serve the customers you attract.

## 6. Keep your budget connected to outcomes

Digital services should be evaluated in relation to the business objective, not simply by the number of deliverables.

A package that includes many pages may not be useful if the business needs only a focused website. A campaign that generates substantial traffic may still disappoint if the visitors are unlikely to buy. An SEO report can identify problems, but the business must decide which changes matter and implement them.

When reviewing proposals, ask:

- What business problem is this work intended to address?
- What will be delivered?
- What must I provide?
- Which costs recur monthly or annually?
- What is outside the agreed scope?
- How will progress be evaluated?
- Who will maintain the work after delivery?

For recurring services, compare the cost with the expected workload and the value of the problem being solved. Avoid relying on guaranteed rankings, guaranteed sales or other promises that cannot be responsibly assured.

A staged plan can be more manageable than a large commitment. For example, improve the website's main service pages, measure enquiries, and then decide whether targeted campaigns or further SEO work are the next priority.

## 7. Practical digital services should fit real South African businesses

Small businesses have different resources, customer groups and operating environments. A business serving customers in central Pretoria may have different needs from one serving customers across Soshanguve, Maboloka or other communities.

Connectivity, mobile usability, customer expectations and the way people contact suppliers should inform digital decisions. Keep pages focused, make contact information easy to find and avoid forcing visitors through unnecessary steps.

Your online information should also be accurate. If you advertise an offer, make its terms clear. If you list service areas, make sure you can genuinely serve them. If you publish examples of past work, ensure they represent real projects and that you have permission to share them.

A credible online presence is built through consistent communication and a reliable customer experience—not simply through frequent posting.

> **Explore digital services:** Visit [Mogen Services](/services) to learn about its web development, SEO and digital marketing services.

## 8. Use a simple 90-day improvement plan

A practical plan can help a business make progress without overextending its budget.

### Days 1–30: establish the foundations

- Review your main business message and service descriptions.
- Check that your website works on mobile devices.
- Verify your contact routes and business details.
- Identify the main customer questions that your website does not answer.
- Choose one or two meaningful measures to track.

### Days 31–60: improve discoverability and clarity

- Update important website pages.
- Improve relevant business listings.
- Publish useful content based on customer questions.
- Remove confusing or outdated information.
- Review available search and website performance data.

### Days 61–90: test and refine

- Identify the pages and channels producing relevant engagement.
- Test a focused marketing activity if it fits your objective and budget.
- Review the quality of enquiries, not just their volume.
- Document what worked and what needs further attention.
- Set the next priorities based on evidence.

This is a planning framework, not a guaranteed growth timeline. The appropriate pace depends on your resources, competition and starting point.

## Why consider Mogen?

Mogen brings together web development, SEO and digital marketing as areas that can support a business's online presence. The sensible starting point is to understand your current needs, identify gaps and choose work that aligns with your objectives.

You do not need to treat every digital service as an immediate purchase. A focused website improvement may be the right first step for one business, while another may need better search visibility or a more structured marketing approach.

The important decision is to choose a clear priority, understand what the work includes and evaluate the outcome honestly.

## Conclusion

Practical digital growth begins with a clear business objective. A useful website gives customers somewhere to understand your offer. SEO can help relevant people discover it. Digital marketing can communicate the offer to a chosen audience. Measurement helps you decide what to improve next.

For growing South African businesses, these activities work best when they are planned around real customer needs, realistic budgets and the capacity to deliver on new enquiries.

Start with the problem that matters most, make a focused improvement and use the results to guide your next decision.

Businesses often invest considerable effort in building marketing databases.

They collect contact details through enquiries, sales, competitions, customer registrations, online forms, events and other interactions.

Over time, these records become valuable marketing assets. They allow businesses to communicate with customers, announce services and promote relevant offers.

But a large database is not necessarily a well-managed database.

Contact details can become outdated. Customers can withdraw permission or object to marketing. Different employees may maintain separate lists, and external agencies may run campaigns without the business having a clear view of which contacts are being used.

[South Africa](/articles/tag/south-africa) is introducing an additional control for [direct marketing](/articles/tag/direct-marketing) through the National Opt-Out Registry.

The National Consumer Commission (NCC) launched the registry on 7 October 2026. It gives consumers a government-administered mechanism to block unwanted direct marketing communication under section 11 of the [Consumer Protection](/articles/tag/consumer-protection) Act.

The rollout is taking place in phases. As at 1 November 2026, direct marketers are in the registration phase, which the NCC says runs from 15 September to December 2026. A five-month list-cleansing phase is planned from December 2026 to April 2027, followed by consumer pre-emptive blocking from May 2027.

For South African businesses, this is a good time to review how marketing lists are collected, stored, updated and used.

The objective is not to stop responsible marketing. It is to ensure that marketing operations respect consumer choices and use contact information appropriately.

## What is the National Opt-Out Registry?

The National Opt-Out Registry is administered by the National Consumer Commission.

It gives consumers a way to register a pre-emptive block against unwanted direct marketing communication.

Section 11 of the Consumer Protection Act provides consumers with rights to restrict unwanted direct marketing. The 2026 amended regulations establish the framework for the NCC to administer the registry.

The NCC describes the registry as a way for consumers to block unwanted direct marketing calls, SMSes and other electronic communication.

Its announcement also refers to email communication when describing the protection the system is intended to provide.

The important change for marketers is that the NCC says direct marketers must register and cleanse their marketing lists monthly before running direct marketing campaigns.

This means that businesses should prepare their marketing processes to account for the registry rather than treating it as an optional database-cleaning exercise.

The official announcement is available from the [National Consumer Commission](https://thencc.org.za/ncc-launches-the-national-opt-out-registry-to-curb-unwanted-direct-marketing/).

## 1. Understand the rollout dates

The registry is being introduced in stages.

The NCC's published rollout provides the following timeline:

| Phase | Period | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Direct marketer registration | 15 September to December 2026 | Direct marketers register with the system |
| List cleansing | December 2026 to April 2027 | Direct marketers receive a five-month period to cleanse lists and prepare for the process |
| Consumer pre-emptive blocking | From May 2027 | Consumers can register blocks against direct marketers |

The NCC states that the list-cleansing period from December to April will be provided at no cost to direct marketers so that they can understand the process and prepare to interface with the system.

The Commission also warns that failure to register during the registration phase may constitute a contravention of section 11 of the CPA, read with the amended regulations.

These dates matter because businesses have an opportunity to prepare their internal systems before consumer blocking begins.

Do not wait until a campaign is about to be sent to discover that the marketing database is disorganised or that nobody knows which supplier is responsible for a contact list.

Review the NCC's latest instructions before registering or making operational decisions, as the Commission may publish further guidance as the rollout progresses.

## 2. Do not confuse the registry with POPIA

One of the most important points for businesses to understand is that the National Opt-Out Registry does not replace [POPIA](/articles/tag/popia).

The Information Regulator addressed this directly in its 21 April 2026 statement following publication of the amended CPA regulations.

It emphasised that POPIA compliance remains mandatory whether or not a consumer has registered a pre-emptive block with the NCC.

This distinction is critical.

A person who has not registered on the new Opt-Out Registry is not automatically available for unsolicited electronic marketing.

POPIA section 69 continues to regulate direct marketing through unsolicited electronic communications.

The Information Regulator explains that direct marketers generally need the data subject's consent or must meet the specific existing-customer exception in section 69(3).

The regulator's statement is available in its [official media statement on the CPA amendment regulations](https://inforegulator.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/MEDIA-STATEMENT-REGULATOR-NOTES-PUBLISHED-GAZETTE-OF-THE-CONSUMER-PROTECT-ACT-AMENDMENT-REGULATIONS-2026.pdf).

The registry and POPIA therefore address related but distinct requirements.

Businesses should not interpret the new system as permission to contact anyone who has not yet registered a block.

## 3. Understand which marketing activities need attention

Direct marketing is not limited to one communication channel.

The Information Regulator's guidance note describes direct marketing as approaching a person in person, by mail or by electronic communication to promote or offer goods or services, or to request a donation.

Its guidance on POPIA section 69 identifies electronic channels including:

- Telephone calls.
- Automatic calling machines.
- Fax.
- SMS.
- Email.

The NCC's registry announcement describes calls, SMSes and other electronic communication.

A business should therefore review its marketing activities across the channels it actually uses.

For example:

| Channel | What to review |
| --- | --- |
| Telephone marketing | Contact lists, call scripts and suppression procedures |
| Bulk SMS | Recipient lists and pre-campaign cleansing |
| Email campaigns | Consent records, objections and suppression lists |
| Messaging platforms | Marketing lists and how opt-out requests are recorded |
| External call centres | Vendor responsibilities and list handling |
| Marketing agencies | Who owns the database and who performs cleansing |
| Customer promotions | Whether the communication is genuinely transactional or promotional |

The purpose of this review is to identify where personal information is used for direct marketing and which processes need to change.

A business should not assume that a campaign is outside the rules simply because it is sent through a different platform.

## 4. Build a complete picture of your marketing database

Before preparing for list cleansing, understand where the business's contact information is stored.

A [small business](/articles/tag/small-business) may have customer details in several places:

- A spreadsheet maintained by the owner.
- A CRM system.
- An accounting or invoicing platform.
- An [email marketing](/articles/tag/email-marketing) platform.
- A bulk SMS provider.
- A website enquiry database.
- A sales team's mobile phones.
- A third-party agency's campaign list.

If these systems are not coordinated, an opt-out request recorded in one place may not reach the other systems.

This creates a practical risk: a customer may ask the business to stop marketing to them, but a separate employee or agency may continue using an older list.

Create an inventory that identifies:

- The system holding the contact information.
- The business purpose for which it is used.
- The communication channels associated with it.
- The person responsible for the system.
- The source of the contact information.
- The applicable consent or other lawful basis.
- How objections and opt-outs are recorded.
- Whether the list is shared with an external provider.

The inventory does not need to be complicated.

A spreadsheet can be a useful starting point for a small business, provided it is maintained and access is controlled.

## 5. Separate marketing consent from customer information

One of the most common database-management mistakes is treating every customer contact detail as permission to send promotional messages.

A person may provide a telephone number because they need a quotation, delivery update or support response.

That interaction does not automatically mean that the business can use the number for every future marketing campaign.

POPIA section 69 provides specific requirements for direct marketing through unsolicited electronic communication.

The Information Regulator's guidance explains that a business may rely on the existing-customer exception only where the relevant conditions are met.

These include:

- The contact details were obtained in the context of a sale of a product or service.
- The marketing concerns the business's own similar products or services.
- The customer was given a reasonable opportunity to object when the details were collected.
- The customer is given an opportunity to object in each subsequent marketing communication if they have not initially refused.

Where consent is required, it must be obtained in the appropriate manner.

The regulator also explains that a business may approach a person once to request consent where the statutory conditions are met and the person has not previously withheld it.

This is not a general permission to repeatedly contact people who have not agreed to receive marketing.

Review the [Information Regulator's Guidance Note on Direct Marketing](https://inforegulator.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/GUIDANCE-NOTE-ON-DIRECT-MARKETING-IN-TERMS-OF-THE-PROTECTION-OF-PERSONAL-INFORMATION-ACT-4-OF-2013-POPIA.pdf) when reviewing these requirements.

## 6. Create a central suppression process

A suppression list records contact details that must not be used for certain marketing activities.

It may include people who have:

- Unsubscribed from email marketing.
- Asked to stop receiving promotional SMS messages.
- Objected to direct marketing.
- Registered a relevant pre-emptive block.
- Withdrawn previously given consent.

The business should have a consistent process for recording and applying these instructions.

For example, if a customer objects to receiving promotional messages, that instruction should not remain only in the inbox of the employee who received it.

It should be reflected in the appropriate marketing systems.

The process should also prevent old lists from being imported again without checking current suppression records.

A central process helps avoid situations where the same customer receives an email from one system after opting out through another.

Be careful about deleting all information associated with an opt-out.

A business may need a minimal record of the objection so that it can continue respecting the person's choice. The way this information is retained should be considered in light of POPIA's requirements for lawful processing, data minimisation and retention.

The business should avoid retaining unnecessary personal information merely because it is easier than maintaining a controlled suppression process.

## 7. Prepare for monthly list cleansing

The NCC says direct marketers must cleanse their lists monthly before running a direct marketing campaign.

This makes list cleansing an operational process rather than an occasional administrative task.

A business should decide who will perform the check, how the result will be recorded and how the cleansed list will reach the people or systems responsible for sending campaigns.

A practical process could look like this:

**Step 1: Identify the campaign**

Record the campaign name, intended audience, communication channel and planned date.

**Step 2: Prepare the recipient list**

Identify the records that will be used for the campaign and confirm their source.

**Step 3: Review internal objections**

Check the business's own unsubscribe and suppression records.

**Step 4: Complete the applicable registry cleansing process**

Follow the current NCC procedure for checking and cleansing the list.

**Step 5: Apply the results**

Ensure that blocked contacts are excluded from the campaign.

**Step 6: Record the outcome**

Keep an appropriate record of the date, list version, process followed and result.

**Step 7: Send only the approved campaign**

Ensure that the final recipient list is the one that passed the checks.

The NCC's phased rollout provides a preparation period for businesses to understand the cleansing process and prepare to interface with the system.

The exact technical workflow should follow the Commission's published instructions rather than assumptions based on another marketing platform.

## 8. Review external marketing providers

Many small businesses use third parties for campaign execution.

These may include:

- Bulk SMS providers.
- Email marketing platforms.
- Call centres.
- Marketing agencies.
- Lead-generation companies.
- CRM and customer-management providers.

Outsourcing a campaign does not remove the need to understand how the contact information is handled.

Ask each provider:

- Where does the recipient list come from?
- Who is responsible for its accuracy?
- How are objections and opt-outs recorded?
- How is the NCC cleansing process handled?
- Can the provider supply evidence of the cleansing process?
- How are campaign lists protected?
- How are outdated or unnecessary records removed?
- What happens when the business ends the contract?

Review the contract or service agreement to establish the responsibilities of each party.

Do not assume that a provider's existing database or registration automatically makes every client campaign compliant.

The business should understand which entity is registering, which lists are being checked and how the results are applied.

## 9. Update campaign templates and employee procedures

A compliant process can still fail when employees use outdated templates or manual lists.

Review the communication templates used by the business.

Under POPIA section 69(4), electronic direct marketing communications must contain the identity of the sender or the person on whose behalf the communication is sent, together with an address or other contact details to which the recipient can send a request that the communication cease.

Ensure that the business's marketing templates contain the appropriate identification and contact information.

Also review:

- Unsubscribe instructions.
- Customer objection procedures.
- Sales scripts.
- Call-centre instructions.
- Campaign approval processes.
- Staff access to marketing lists.
- Procedures for importing new contacts.
- Training for employees who collect customer details.

Employees should know the difference between recording a customer enquiry and adding someone to a marketing database.

A clear procedure reduces the risk of staff making inconsistent decisions.

## 10. Keep evidence of marketing decisions

A business should be able to explain where a contact came from and why it was included in a campaign.

This does not mean retaining every piece of personal information indefinitely.

It means maintaining appropriate records that support accountability.

Depending on the business and its processes, useful records may include:

- The source of the contact information.
- The date and method of consent where consent is required.
- The relevant customer relationship where the existing-customer exception is used.
- The date an objection was received.
- The date a contact was suppressed.
- The campaign for which a list was prepared.
- The date the NCC cleansing process was completed.
- The identity of the person approving the campaign.
- The external provider involved.

Access to these records should be restricted to people who need them.

The business should also define how long the records are retained and when they are reviewed or securely disposed of.

## 11. What this means for smaller South African businesses

A small business does not need a large marketing department to prepare for the registry.

It does need a clear process.

Consider a service business that promotes its offerings to customers in [Maboloka](/locations/maboloka), [Soshanguve](/locations/soshanguve), [Centurion](/locations/centurion) and surrounding areas.

It may have contact details collected through website enquiries, WhatsApp conversations, previous customers and local campaigns.

If each source is maintained separately, the business may struggle to apply customer objections consistently.

A practical starting point is to bring the lists into a controlled system, identify the source and purpose of each contact, and establish one process for recording marketing preferences.

The business can then prepare its campaign workflow for the NCC cleansing process.

This is useful even when the business sends only occasional promotional messages.

A small database can still contain outdated details, withdrawn permissions and records that should not be used for marketing.

## 12. A practical preparation checklist

Use this checklist to review your current direct marketing operations:

- [ ] Identify every system containing marketing contacts.
- [ ] Identify all channels used for direct marketing.
- [ ] Confirm the source of each contact list.
- [ ] Review the applicable consent or lawful basis.
- [ ] Separate customer-service records from marketing preferences.
- [ ] Create a central process for recording objections.
- [ ] Prevent suppressed contacts from being re-imported.
- [ ] Identify external agencies and campaign providers.
- [ ] Review provider responsibilities and contracts.
- [ ] Follow the NCC's current registration instructions.
- [ ] Prepare for the December 2026 to April 2027 cleansing phase.
- [ ] Establish a monthly pre-campaign cleansing procedure.
- [ ] Update marketing templates and contact details.
- [ ] Train employees who collect or use customer information.
- [ ] Keep appropriate evidence of campaign preparation.
- [ ] Review the process whenever a new channel or provider is introduced.

> **Marketing assessment:**
>
> If your business uses several marketing channels or maintains multiple customer lists, start with a [Mogen assessment](/#assessment) to review your current digital business setup.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is the National Opt-Out Registry already fully operational?

No. The NCC has announced a phased rollout. Direct marketer registration opened on 15 September 2026 and runs until December 2026. The list-cleansing phase is planned for December 2026 to April 2027, with consumer pre-emptive blocking expected from May 2027.

### Does a business have to register as a direct marketer?

The NCC states that direct marketers must register with the system. Businesses conducting direct marketing should review the Commission's current registration instructions and complete the applicable process within the published phase.

### Does the registry replace POPIA consent requirements?

No. The Information Regulator has explicitly stated that POPIA compliance remains mandatory whether or not a consumer has registered a pre-emptive block. POPIA section 69 continues to regulate direct marketing through unsolicited electronic communication.

### Does the registry only apply to telephone calls?

The NCC describes the registry in terms of calls, SMSes and other electronic communication, and its launch statement also refers to emails. Businesses should review all the channels they use and follow the NCC's published guidance.

### Can I market to an existing customer?

POPIA section 69(3) provides a specific existing-customer exception subject to conditions. These include how the contact details were obtained, the similarity of the products or services being marketed and the customer's opportunity to object. A business should not assume that every previous customer can automatically receive every promotional message.

### What happens during the cleansing phase?

The NCC has announced a five-month period from December 2026 to April 2027 during which direct marketers can cleanse their lists at no cost and prepare to interface with the system. Businesses should follow the Commission's current technical instructions.

> **[Digital marketing](/services/digital-marketing):**
>
> Visit the [Mogen promotions page](/promotions) to review currently published offers before planning your next digital marketing project.

## Conclusion

South Africa's National Opt-Out Registry is an important development for businesses that use direct marketing.

The rollout gives marketers time to review their registration, customer databases, campaign processes and relationships with external providers.

The most important preparation is to stop treating marketing lists as static spreadsheets that can be reused indefinitely.

Businesses need to know where their contact information comes from, why it is being used, how objections are recorded and how those decisions are applied before campaigns are sent.

The registry does not replace POPIA. It adds another requirement to an environment where responsible direct marketing already depends on respecting customer choices and handling personal information appropriately.

Start by understanding your current lists and channels. Then follow the NCC's registration and cleansing instructions, document the process and make sure everyone involved in marketing understands their responsibilities.
